practice_questions.text: State the difference between mass and weight.
practice_questions.marks: Mass is the amount of matter in an object (measured in kg); weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass (measured in N). [1 mark — must distinguish units or scalar/vector nature]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a free-body diagram shows and what the arrows in a free-body diagram represent.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Identifies that a free-body diagram shows forces on an object.
Secure: States that arrows show the direction of each force (1 mark); arrow length represents the magnitude (size) of the force (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why an astronaut has less weight on the Moon than on Earth, even though their mass is the same. Use the equation W = mg in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: States that gravity is weaker on the Moon.
Developing: Identifies that the Moon has a lower gravitational field strength (g) than Earth (1 mark).
Secure: Uses W = mg to show that with the same mass (m), a smaller g gives a smaller weight W (1 mark). Clarifies that mass does not change because it depends only on the amount of matter, not location (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A 70 kg cyclist and their 15 kg bicycle are moving along a flat road. Pedalling produces a forward force of 500 N. Friction and air resistance together produce a backward force of 200 N. Calculate the resultant force on the cyclist and bicycle system, then suggest what would happen to their motion.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Identifies that resultant force = 500 − 200 = 300 N forwards (1 mark).
Secure: States that because there is an unbalanced resultant force, the system will accelerate (1 mark).
Mastering: Calculates acceleration using F = ma: total mass = 70 + 15 = 85 kg; a = 300/85 ≈ 3.5 m/s² (1 mark). Suggests the cyclist continues to speed up until air resistance increases enough to balance the forward force, after which the cyclist moves at a constant top speed (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A book rests on a table. Identify the Newton's Third Law force pair for the weight of the book acting on Earth, and explain why the weight of the book and the normal contact force from the table are NOT a Newton's Third Law pair.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Identifies that Newton’s Third Law pairs act on different objects.
Secure: Correctly identifies the Third Law pair for weight: the book pulls the Earth upwards with a gravitational force equal and opposite to its weight (1 mark). This force acts on the Earth, not the book (1 mark).
Mastering: Explains that weight and normal contact force are NOT a Third Law pair because they both act on the same object (the book) (1 mark); also, they are different types of force — weight is gravitational, normal contact force is mechanical — whereas Third Law pairs must be the same type of force (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of correctly distinguishing between mass and weight in real-world scientific contexts. Use at least two specific examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: States that mass and weight are different and have different units.
Developing: Explains that mass is constant everywhere (kg) and weight depends on gravitational field strength (N) using W = mg (1 mark). Gives one relevant example, such as space engineering (1 mark).
Secure: Provides two specific examples, e.g. (1) spacecraft design — engineers must account for the different weight of the craft on different planets even though mass is unchanged (1 mark); (2) medical measurement — clinical drug doses are calculated by mass (kg) not weight, because mass is constant regardless of where the patient is measured (1 mark).
Mastering: Evaluates the consequences of confusing the two — e.g. a spacecraft calibrated for Earth weight but used on Mars would have incorrect thrust calculations; a drug dose based on weight in newtons would vary by location and could cause harm. Reaches a reasoned conclusion about why the distinction matters scientifically and practically (2 further marks). [6 marks — levels marked]

practice_questions.text: State what magnification means.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The number of times larger the image appears compared with the actual object / the ratio of image size to actual size.
Secure: Image is larger than real object by a set amount.
Developing: Something about the image being bigger.
Emerging: Vague or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: A plant cell is drawn in a biology textbook. The drawn width of the cell is 36 mm and the actual width of the cell is 0.09 mm. Calculate the magnification used. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size = 36 ÷ 0.09 = ×400. (Both marks: correct formula applied + correct answer.)
Secure: Correct formula and method but minor arithmetic error; or correct answer with insufficient working shown.
Developing: Formula recalled but values substituted incorrectly.
Emerging: Attempt at calculation but no correct formula shown.

practice_questions.text: An electron microscope image shows a mitochondrion with a drawn length of 60 mm. The magnification is ×12,000. Calculate the actual length of the mitochondrion in micrometres (µm). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification = 60 ÷ 12,000 = 0.005 mm; convert: 0.005 mm × 1,000 = 5 µm. (All three marks: rearrangement [1], calculation in mm [1], correct conversion to µm [1].)
Secure: Correct rearrangement and calculation but conversion step missing or minor error.
Developing: Rearrangement attempted but magnification used as multiplier rather than divisor.
Emerging: Some values substituted but no clear method.

practice_questions.text: Convert the following measurements: (a) 0.25 mm into µm; (b) 8,500 nm into µm; (c) 2 µm into nm.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) 250 µm; (b) 8.5 µm; (c) 2,000 nm. (One mark per correct answer.)
Secure: Two out of three correct.
Developing: One correct conversion; others show confusion between × and ÷ steps.
Emerging: Attempts made but all conversions incorrect.

practice_questions.text: A student uses a light microscope and then an electron microscope to study a cell. Suggest two advantages of using an electron microscope rather than a light microscope when studying organelles such as mitochondria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two advantages, each with explanation: (1) Higher magnification — electron microscopes can magnify far more than light microscopes, so organelles appear larger and more detail is visible. (2) Greater resolution — electron microscopes can distinguish between structures that are very close together, whereas light microscopes cannot; this means individual features of organelles (e.g. cristae of mitochondria) can be seen. [2 marks per advantage: 1 for the advantage, 1 for the explanation.]
Secure: Two advantages stated with partial explanation.
Developing: One advantage with explanation, or two advantages without explanation.
Emerging: One advantage stated without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A scientist claims that the development of the electron microscope was essential for improving our understanding of sub-cellular structures. Evaluate this claim, referring to the limitations of light microscopes and the types of evidence that electron microscopy provided.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates both sides clearly. Arguments for: electron microscopes provide magnification up to ×1,000,000 (vs ~×1,500 for light), enabling detailed images of organelles; resolution is high enough to show internal structure of mitochondria (cristae) and chloroplasts (grana); this led to understanding of how structure relates to function; light microscopes cannot resolve structures closer than about 200 nm, so organelles below this size are invisible. Balancing point: light microscopes allow study of living cells; electron microscopes require dead, stained specimens. Conclusion: the claim is well-supported — electron microscopy genuinely transformed understanding that was impossible before its development. Uses evaluative language throughout.
Secure: Both types of microscope discussed with relevant points; some attempt at evaluative conclusion.
Developing: Descriptive comparison with limited evaluation.
Emerging: One or two relevant points about microscopes with no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: State where aerobic respiration takes place in a cell.
practice_questions.marks: Mitochondria. (1 mark. Accept 'mitochondrion'.)

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in terms of oxygen and ATP yield.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen and produces a large yield of ATP because glucose is completely broken down. Anaerobic respiration does not require oxygen and produces a much smaller yield of ATP because glucose is only partially broken down.
Secure: Aerobic uses oxygen, high ATP; anaerobic no oxygen, low ATP.
Developing: Aerobic needs oxygen; anaerobic does not.
Emerging: One correct point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a runner continues to breathe heavily for several minutes after finishing a sprint race.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During the sprint, muscles worked anaerobically because oxygen could not be supplied fast enough. This produced lactic acid in the muscles. After the race, the runner continues to breathe heavily to supply extra oxygen, which is used by the liver to convert accumulated lactic acid back to glucose. This is the repayment of the oxygen debt.
Secure: Lactic acid built up during the race; extra oxygen is needed afterwards to break it down.
Developing: Lactic acid built up; needs more oxygen to break it down.
Emerging: The body needs more oxygen.

practice_questions.text: Compare the products of anaerobic respiration in a human muscle cell and in a yeast cell.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a human muscle cell, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid (and a small amount of ATP). In a yeast cell, anaerobic respiration (fermentation) produces ethanol and carbon dioxide (and a small amount of ATP). Both processes share the same reactant (glucose) and both occur in the cytoplasm without oxygen, but their products differ because of different metabolic pathways.
Secure: Muscle → lactic acid; yeast → ethanol + carbon dioxide. Both need no oxygen and produce little ATP.
Developing: Muscle makes lactic acid; yeast makes ethanol and CO₂.
Emerging: One correct product for either organism.

practice_questions.text: A student measures the temperature inside two sealed flasks over 30 minutes. Flask A contains germinating pea seeds; Flask B contains the same mass of boiled (dead) pea seeds. Suggest why the student includes Flask B in the investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Flask B is a control. It shows any temperature change that occurs without biological respiration (e.g. from chemical processes in dead cells or heat from the environment). Comparing Flask A with Flask B allows the student to confirm that any additional temperature rise in Flask A is due to respiration by the living seeds, not to another variable. Without the control, any conclusion about respiration would be unreliable.
Secure: Flask B is a control to show what happens without living seeds, so any difference in Flask A can be attributed to respiration.
Developing: It is a control so you can compare.
Emerging: It is the control.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of fermentation by yeast in two commercial industries. For each, explain both the benefit of the fermentation process and any limitation or risk.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In bread-making, yeast ferments sugars to produce CO₂, which makes dough rise creating a light texture — the ethanol produced evaporates during baking. A limitation is temperature control: too cold and yeast respires too slowly; too hot and the yeast is killed. In brewing, yeast ferments sugars in grain or fruit juice to produce ethanol for alcoholic drinks. A limitation is that if ethanol concentration rises too high, it becomes toxic to the yeast, halting fermentation. Both industries exploit anaerobic respiration but need careful management of conditions.
Secure: Two industries described with a correct fermentation product for each; one benefit and one limitation per industry.
Developing: Two industries described with products; limited evaluation.
Emerging: One industry described correctly.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a delocalised electron.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: electron that is free to move throughout the whole metallic structure / not associated with a single atom. Secure: free electron. Developing: electron in the sea. Emerging: vague reference to electrons.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of a giant ionic lattice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: positive and negative ions arranged in a regular three-dimensional lattice held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions. Secure: oppositely charged ions in a regular lattice held by electrostatic forces. Developing: ions held together by attraction. Emerging: particles arranged in rows.

practice_questions.text: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. Both are forms of carbon.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: in graphite each carbon forms three covalent bonds, leaving one electron per carbon delocalised and free to move and carry charge; in diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds so all electrons are used and none are free. Secure: graphite has delocalised/free electrons; diamond does not because all electrons are bonded. Developing: graphite has free electrons. Emerging: graphite is a different form of carbon.

practice_questions.text: Compare the electrical conductivity of sodium chloride in the solid state with sodium chloride dissolved in water. Explain the difference.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: solid does not conduct because ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot carry charge; dissolved in water the lattice is broken down and ions are free to move and carry an electric current, so it does conduct. Secure: solid = ions fixed, no conduction; dissolved = ions free to move, conducts. Developing: dissolved conducts because it has ions. Emerging: solid is different from liquid.

practice_questions.text: A student wants to select a material for making the inner filament of a light bulb. The filament must withstand very high temperatures, conduct electricity, and not shatter under mechanical stress. Evaluate which type of bonding and structure would be most suitable, justifying your answer using evidence from the properties of different bond types.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies metallic bonding as most suitable; explains high melting point from strong attraction between ions and electron sea; explains conductivity from delocalised electrons; explains resistance to shattering from malleability (layers slide without breaking); contrasts with ionic (brittle, only conducts when molten), giant covalent (non-conductor except graphite, very hard but brittle), simple molecular (far too low melting point). Secure: correct identification of metals with two well-explained properties and one contrast. Developing: identifies metals with one property explained. Emerging: names metals without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why simple molecular substances such as water have much lower melting points than giant ionic compounds such as sodium chloride.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: simple molecular substances have weak intermolecular forces between molecules which require little energy to overcome, so they melt at low temperatures; ionic compounds have many strong electrostatic forces between ions in all directions which require a large amount of energy to break, so they have high melting points. Secure: weak intermolecular forces vs strong electrostatic forces, with reference to energy. Developing: simple molecules have weak forces, ionic have strong forces. Emerging: simple molecules are smaller.

practice_questions.text: A ball of mass 0.5 kg is travelling at 6 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
Describe what happens to the stores of energy when a ball is thrown vertically upwards and then falls back to its starting height. Ignore air resistance.
practice_questions.marks: As the ball rises, kinetic energy decreases and gravitational potential energy increases by the same amount [1 mark]. As it falls, GPE converts back to KE; at the starting height the KE equals the original value [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that KE converts to GPE (or vice versa) but does not address both directions or conservation.

practice_questions.text: A crane lifts a 200 kg steel beam vertically by 15 m in 30 seconds. Calculate the power output of the crane's motor. (g = 10 N/kg)
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Attempts GPE or power calculation but makes an error in one step.

practice_questions.text: A car of mass 1,200 kg accelerates from rest to a speed of 20 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy gained. Then suggest why the engine must supply more energy than this value during the acceleration.
practice_questions.marks: E_k = 0.5 × 1200 × 20² = 0.5 × 1200 × 400 = 240,000 J [2 marks]. The engine must supply more energy because some energy is transferred to the surroundings by friction (between tyres and road and within engine parts) and by air resistance, so not all the engine's energy output becomes useful kinetic energy [1 mark — any suitable reason]. Dissipated energy ends up as thermal energy in the surroundings [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct KE and identifies one energy loss mechanism.
Developing: Correct KE but does not explain energy loss, or vice versa.

practice_questions.text: A rollercoaster car of mass 800 kg is at the top of a drop at a height of 45 m above the ground. It starts from rest. Calculate the speed of the car at the bottom of the drop, assuming no energy is lost to friction or air resistance. (g = 10 N/kg)
practice_questions.marks: GPE at top = mgh = 800 × 10 × 45 = 360,000 J [1 mark]. This all converts to KE at the bottom: ½mv² = 360,000, so v² = (2 × 360,000) ÷ 800 = 900 [1 mark]; v = √900 = 30 m/s [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Calculates GPE correctly but cannot rearrange KE equation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'a heavier car is always more dangerous in a collision than a lighter car at the same speed.' Use physics to support and challenge this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Calculates or compares KE using E_k = ½mv² for both cases; notes that at the same speed a heavier car has greater KE so more energy must be dissipated in a collision (supports the claim). Challenges by noting that speed is squared — a lighter car at twice the speed has four times the KE of the heavier car at the original speed, so speed is actually more significant than mass. Reaches a justified conclusion: the statement is partially true but speed is the dominant factor because of the v² relationship.
Secure: Correctly identifies KE depends on both mass and speed; compares the effect qualitatively; some reference to the equation.
Developing: Identifies that both mass and speed affect KE but does not use the equation to evaluate relative importance.
Emerging: States that heavier objects are more dangerous with no reference to KE equation.

practice_questions.text: Name the gas that was most abundant in Earth's early atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks: Carbon dioxide. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how photosynthesis changed the composition of Earth's early atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Photosynthesis by early organisms absorbed carbon dioxide (1) and released oxygen into the atmosphere (1).
Secure: Oxygen increased and carbon dioxide decreased due to photosynthesis (2).
Developing: States photosynthesis produced oxygen (1).
Emerging: Vague (0).

practice_questions.text: Explain three ways in which carbon dioxide was removed from Earth's early atmosphere over billions of years.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Photosynthesis by plants/cyanobacteria absorbed CO2 and released oxygen (1); CO2 dissolved in the oceans (1); marine organisms used dissolved CO2 to make calcium carbonate shells, which eventually became sedimentary rocks (limestone) or fossil fuels (1).
Secure: Any two clearly explained routes (2).
Developing: One route (1).
Emerging: States CO2 decreased without mechanism (0).

practice_questions.text: Scientists cannot directly sample Earth's atmosphere from 4 billion years ago. Suggest two types of evidence they use to support their claims about the early atmosphere, and explain what each type of evidence tells us.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Ancient rocks — composition reveals what gases were present when the rock formed, e.g. absence of oxidised iron minerals suggests no free oxygen (1+1). Fossils of early life — fossils of the first photosynthesising organisms show when oxygen production began (1+1). [Also credit: volcanic emissions, planetary comparison.]
Secure: Two types of evidence with some explanation of what each shows (2–3).
Developing: One type of evidence named but not explained (1).
Emerging: Vague (0).

practice_questions.text: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the current atmosphere. It was not removed from the early atmosphere in the same way that carbon dioxide was. Suggest why nitrogen became the dominant atmospheric gas over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Nitrogen is relatively unreactive (1); it does not take part in photosynthesis (1); it does not dissolve in oceans or form sedimentary rocks (1); as carbon dioxide decreased through these processes, nitrogen became the dominant gas by proportion (1).
Secure: Two of the above with a clear reasoning step (2–3).
Developing: States nitrogen is unreactive (1).
Emerging: Vague (0).

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how scientists develop an understanding of Earth's ancient atmosphere when direct evidence is unavailable. In your answer, consider the types of evidence used, what each tells us and the limitations of each. Reach a conclusion about the overall reliability of our current understanding.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evidence types — ancient rocks (record chemical conditions, but interpretation requires assumptions about how rocks form) (1); ice cores (direct air samples but only go back ~800,000 years, not billions) (1); volcanic emissions (show what gases volcanoes produce today, but may not exactly mirror ancient volcanoes) (1); planetary comparison with Mars and Venus (supportive circumstantial evidence but those planets had different geological histories) (1). Conclusion — no single source is definitive, but multiple independent sources that all support the same picture gives high overall confidence (1). Quality of evaluative reasoning throughout (1).
Secure: Three evidence types with at least one limitation and a conclusion (4–5).
Developing: Two evidence types without engaging with limitations (2–3).
Emerging: One evidence type listed (1).

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by background radiation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: radiation from natural and artificial sources that forms a constant low-level exposure for everyone on Earth [accept: radiation present in the environment / from rocks, cosmic rays, radon gas, food, medical procedures].

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between contamination and irradiation as sources of radiation exposure.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: contamination means radioactive material is on or inside the body, giving continuous exposure. 1 mark: irradiation means exposure to an external source; the exposure stops when the source is removed / the person does not become radioactive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why technetium-99m (half-life approximately 6 hours) is a suitable isotope for use as a medical tracer rather than an isotope with a half-life of several years.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: it emits gamma radiation, which penetrates the body and can be detected externally. 1 mark: the short half-life means the isotope decays quickly inside the body. 1 mark: so the patient receives a much lower total radiation dose than with a long-lived isotope [OR: the radioactivity drops to safe levels within hours/days].

practice_questions.text: A doctor recommends a CT scan (which uses X-rays) for a 65-year-old patient to check for a suspected tumour. Compare the benefits and risks of this procedure for this patient.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): clearly states the benefit (imaging can detect a tumour enabling treatment); explains the risk mechanism (X-rays are ionising and can damage DNA / increase cancer risk slightly); gives context for both (early cancer detection at this age is life-saving; a small additional cancer risk is acceptable given this benefit); reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure (3): identifies benefit and risk with some explanation; partial contextualisation.
Developing (2): lists a benefit and a risk without explaining or weighing them.
Emerging (1): states one correct point.

practice_questions.text: Smoke detectors use alpha radiation from a sealed source inside the device. Evaluate whether this represents a safe use of radioactive material, using your knowledge of alpha radiation properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): explains alpha's short range in air and inability to penetrate the detector casing (so external exposure is negligible); explains the ionisation mechanism that makes the detector work; considers the contamination scenario — if the seal were broken and alpha source ingested or inhaled, the risk would be much greater (alpha is strongly ionising inside tissue); weighs the negligible risk against the substantial benefit (early fire warning saves lives); reaches a justified conclusion that the use is safe in normal conditions.
Secure (3–4): covers most points with some explanation.
Developing (2): identifies alpha cannot penetrate and detector is useful but doesn't evaluate the sealed-source argument or contamination scenario.
Emerging (1): states one relevant fact.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a radiotherapy patient might receive radiation from several different angles rather than one beam directed at a tumour.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: each beam delivers a dose to the surrounding healthy tissue as it passes through to reach the tumour. 1 mark: using multiple angles means each area of healthy tissue only receives a fraction of the total dose. 1 mark: the tumour receives the full combined dose from all angles / maximises damage to tumour while minimising harm to healthy cells.

before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on radiation risk and benefit, the mark scheme rewards evaluation: you must identify the specific benefit in the given scenario (what the radiation does and why it helps), identify the specific risk (which type of radiation, which cells are at risk and why), then reach a justified conclusion. Simply listing “benefits: cures cancer; risks: causes cancer” will not score highly — you need to explain the science behind each point and weigh them against each other. The ‘Suggest’ command word means you should apply the science to the context given in the question, not just recall general facts.

practice_questions.text: Calculate the relative formula mass (M<sub>r</sub>) of sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. (A<sub>r</sub>: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16.)
practice_questions.marks: Award: M<sub>r</sub> = (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 98. Accept correct calculation only.

practice_questions.text: How many moles are present in 8 g of magnesium? (A<sub>r</sub> of Mg = 24.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: moles equation stated and correct answer 0.33 mol (or 1/3 mol) with unit.
Secure: correct method, minor rounding error accepted.
Developing: equation recalled but numerical error.
Emerging: equation not recalled.

practice_questions.text: A sample contains 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate (CaCO<sub>3</sub>, M<sub>r</sub> = 100). Calculate the mass of the sample and explain what is meant by one mole.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mass = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g (1), one mole defined as 6.0 × 10²³ particles (1), links mole to mass using M<sub>r</sub> (1).
Secure: correct mass, definition incomplete.
Developing: mass correct but mole not defined.
Emerging: partial attempt at calculation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the percentage by mass of nitrogen in two fertilisers: ammonium nitrate (NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>, M<sub>r</sub> = 80) and urea (CO(NH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, M<sub>r</sub> = 60). Which contains a higher percentage of nitrogen? (A<sub>r</sub>: N = 14.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> has 2 N atoms: percentage = (2 × 14 ÷ 80) × 100 = 35% (1); urea has 2 N atoms: percentage = (2 × 14 ÷ 60) × 100 = 46.7% (1); correct comparison that urea has higher nitrogen content (1); correct method shown for both (1).
Secure: both percentages correct, comparison stated.
Developing: one correct percentage, method shown.
Emerging: percentage equation stated but not applied correctly.

practice_questions.text: When 2.4 g of magnesium ribbon is burned in air, 4.0 g of magnesium oxide is formed. Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted. Explain whether mass has been conserved in this reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mass of oxygen = 4.0 − 2.4 = 1.6 g (1), mass is conserved because no atoms are created or destroyed (1), the extra mass came from oxygen in the air combining with magnesium (1).
Secure: correct mass of oxygen, partial explanation.
Developing: mass calculated but explanation incomplete.
Emerging: calculation only or explanation only.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates the reaction of calcium carbonate with acid. The student measures the mass of the flask and contents at the start and end and finds the total mass has decreased. Using your knowledge of chemical reactions and conservation of mass, explain this observation and suggest how the experiment could be modified to demonstrate that mass is actually conserved.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mass conservation stated as a principle (1), identifies CO<sub>2</sub> gas escaping as the cause of apparent mass decrease (2), modification suggested e.g. collecting gas or using a sealed system (1), clear explanation that if gas is captured the total mass would be unchanged (2).
Secure: principle stated, gas escape identified, modification present but not fully justified.
Developing: gas escape mentioned, limited explanation.
Emerging: identifies a mass change without scientific explanation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'genome'.
practice_questions.marks: The complete genetic material (DNA) of an organism. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of DNA, including the role of base pairing.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: DNA is a double helix polymer made of two nucleotide strands. The strands are held together by complementary base pairs (A-T and C-G). [2 marks — 1 for double helix/polymer structure, 1 for complementary base pairing rule.]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a change in a gene's base sequence could affect the protein it codes for.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A change in the base sequence alters the triplet code; a different triplet codes for a different amino acid, so the amino acid sequence changes; this alters the folded shape of the protein, changing or destroying its function.
Secure: Altered base sequence → different amino acid sequence → different protein shape.
Developing: Altered sequence → different protein made.
Emerging: Change in DNA → change in protein.

practice_questions.text: Compare the genotype and phenotype of two individuals who both have brown eyes but different allele combinations for eye colour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Individual A may be homozygous for the brown allele (BB); individual B may be heterozygous (Bb). Both have the same phenotype (brown eyes) because brown is dominant over blue, so the presence of even one B allele produces the brown phenotype. Their genotypes differ despite the same phenotype.
Secure: Different genotypes (BB and Bb) → same phenotype because brown allele is dominant.
Developing: One has two brown alleles; the other has one of each; both look the same.
Emerging: They have different alleles but the same eye colour.

practice_questions.text: A person receives their consumer genome report and discovers they carry a variant associated with increased risk of a particular condition. Explain why this does not mean they will definitely develop the condition, and describe one way this information could be used beneficially.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Many conditions are polygenic — multiple genes contribute — so one variant alone rarely determines outcome. Environmental factors (diet, exercise, exposure) also interact with genotype to shape phenotype. Beneficial use: the person could adopt lifestyle changes to reduce their environmental risk, or attend regular screening so any early signs are caught and treated promptly.
Secure: One variant doesn't guarantee illness because environment and other genes also matter; benefit — early screening or lifestyle changes.
Developing: Other things also cause the condition; they could go to the doctor more often.
Emerging: It's just a risk, not certain.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the benefits and limitations of using the human genome sequence to develop personalised medicine for inherited conditions.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluates both sides with science. Benefits — identifying specific gene variants linked to conditions enables targeted drug selection and dosing; reduces trial-and-error prescribing; enables predictive genetic testing so at-risk individuals can take preventive action. Limitations — many conditions are polygenic and environmentally influenced, so genomic data alone cannot predict outcomes reliably; sequencing costs and data interpretation require specialist infrastructure; raises ethical questions about genetic privacy and insurance discrimination. Reaches a balanced conclusion weighing evidence.
Secure: Clear benefits (targeted treatment, early detection) and limitations (complexity, cost, ethics) with some development of each.
Developing: Lists a few benefits and limitations without linking to the science.
Emerging: One benefit and one limitation stated only.

practice_questions.text: State the equation for efficiency.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = useful energy transferred ÷ total energy transferred [1 mark]. Accept: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input.

practice_questions.text: A light bulb takes in 60 J of electrical energy each second and transfers 12 J as light. Calculate its efficiency and state how much energy is wasted each second.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = 12 ÷ 60 = 0.2 (or 20%) [1 mark]. Wasted energy = 60 − 12 = 48 J per second (48 W wasted as thermal energy) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain how fitting a car engine with better lubrication improves its efficiency. Refer to energy stores in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts [1 mark]. Less energy is therefore transferred to the thermal store of the engine (wasted as heat) [1 mark]. So a greater fraction of the chemical energy from fuel is transferred usefully as kinetic energy, increasing efficiency [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that lubrication reduces friction and improves efficiency but does not link to energy stores.

practice_questions.text: A wind turbine has a power input of 8,000 W from the wind and a useful electrical power output of 2,800 W. Calculate the efficiency. Compare this with a coal-fired power station that operates at 35% efficiency. Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of using the wind turbine instead.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = 2800 ÷ 8000 = 0.35 (35%) [1 mark]. Both operate at the same efficiency [1 mark]. Advantage: wind is a renewable resource so will not run out; no carbon dioxide emissions [1 mark — any valid advantage]. Disadvantage: wind turbines only generate when wind is blowing (intermittent supply); output depends on wind speed [1 mark — any valid disadvantage].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct efficiency, correct comparison, one advantage and one disadvantage.
Developing: Correct efficiency but comparison or advantage/disadvantage incomplete.

practice_questions.text: A device has a total energy input of 500 J. Its Sankey diagram shows two output arrows: a useful output of 350 J and a wasted output. Calculate the efficiency of the device.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = 350 ÷ 500 = 0.70 (or 70%) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'improving the efficiency of energy devices is the most important step we can take to address energy resource depletion.' Use your knowledge of efficiency and energy resources to argue both for and against this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues for — higher efficiency means less total energy input is needed for the same useful output, so non-renewable resources last longer; uses efficiency equation to show that higher efficiency = less wasted energy; applies to specific examples (LEDs vs filament bulbs, electric motors vs combustion engines). Argues against — even a perfectly efficient device still uses an energy resource; switching to renewable sources removes dependence on depletable resources entirely; demand management and lifestyle changes may be equally important. Reaches a justified conclusion: improving efficiency is important but insufficient on its own.
Secure: Presents arguments on both sides with some reference to efficiency or energy resources.
Developing: Identifies efficiency as relevant but gives one-sided answer.
Emerging: Simple assertion without use of physics concepts.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'heterozygous'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Having two different alleles of a gene (e.g. Bb).
Secure: Two different versions of the gene / allele.
Developing: One dominant and one recessive — credit if linked to alleles.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: In guinea pigs, the allele for black fur (B) is dominant over the allele for white fur (b). Two heterozygous guinea pigs are crossed. Construct a Punnett square and state the expected phenotype ratio of the offspring.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Punnett square correctly drawn with parental gametes B and b along top and side (1 mark). Grid filled correctly: BB, Bb, Bb, bb (1 mark). Phenotype ratio stated as 3 black : 1 white (1 mark).
Secure: Correct Punnett square and ratio but genotype and phenotype ratio confused.
Developing: Grid attempted but one or more cells incorrect; ratio stated.
Emerging: Parental genotypes written but no grid drawn.

practice_questions.text: A heterozygous guinea pig (Bb) is crossed with a homozygous recessive guinea pig (bb). Describe the expected genotype ratio and calculate the probability (as a percentage) that an offspring will show the dominant phenotype.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Punnett square giving Bb, Bb, bb, bb. Genotype ratio Bb : bb = 1 : 1 (1 mark). Dominant phenotype (Bb) occurs in 2 out of 4 cells = 50% probability (1 mark). Clear working shown (1 mark).
Secure: Correct ratio and probability but working not clearly shown.
Developing: Correct ratio but probability calculated incorrectly.
Emerging: Punnett square attempted with errors; ratio guessed.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Punnett squares give expected rather than guaranteed outcomes. Use the term 'probability' in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Punnett squares predict the probability of each genotype based on random combination of gametes during fertilisation. Because fertilisation is a random process, actual outcomes may differ from the predicted ratio, especially if the sample size is small. The more offspring produced, the closer results are likely to match the predicted ratio. (Award marks for: probability/randomness of fertilisation [1], link to sample size [1], conclusion about actual vs expected [1].)
Secure: Randomness and probability explained, some reference to sample size.
Developing: States that actual results may differ but does not explain why.
Emerging: Brief or vague reference to chance.

practice_questions.text: A genetic disorder is caused by a recessive allele (d). A child is born with the disorder. Both parents appear unaffected. Suggest, with reasoning, the likely genotypes of both parents.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Child must have genotype dd (two recessive alleles, one from each parent). Since parents are unaffected, they each show the dominant phenotype; they cannot be dd. For each parent to pass on a d allele without showing the disorder, they must be heterozygous (Dd) carriers. Conclusion: both parents are Dd. Punnett square (Dd × Dd) confirms dd offspring is possible (25% probability). [4 marks: child's genotype dd [1]; reason parents must be carriers [1]; both parent genotypes stated as Dd [1]; supporting Punnett square or probability [1].]
Secure: Parents identified as Dd with valid reasoning; minor error in probability statement.
Developing: Parents identified as carriers but reasoning incomplete.
Emerging: Attempt at reasoning with genotype errors.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of Punnett squares as models for predicting genetic outcomes. In your answer, refer to both the strengths and limitations of the model.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Strengths: Punnett squares provide a clear, structured method for predicting expected genotype and phenotype ratios for single-gene crosses; they model the random nature of gamete combination and enable probability calculations; they are widely used in medicine to predict risk of inherited disorders; they connect to established genetic theory (Mendelian inheritance). Limitations: they only model single-gene inheritance; most real characteristics are controlled by many genes and are also influenced by the environment, so a Punnett square for height or skin colour would be inaccurate; results are theoretical probabilities, not guaranteed outcomes — small sample sizes may give very different ratios; the model assumes all gametes are equally viable and that fertilisation is completely random, which may not always hold true. Conclusion: a strong model for simple inheritance but not suitable for complex multi-gene traits or predicting outcomes for individual pregnancies. Uses evaluative language throughout.
Secure: Both strengths and limitations addressed with relevant examples; some evaluative language.
Developing: Strengths or limitations described but not evaluated; limited range of points.
Emerging: One relevant point with little development or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'carrier' of a recessive genetic condition.
practice_questions.marks: An individual who carries one copy of the recessive allele but does not show the condition (heterozygous). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a Punnett square is used for and how it is constructed.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: A Punnett square predicts the possible genotypes (and phenotypes) of offspring. One parent's alleles are placed along the top; the other parent's alleles along the side; each box shows one possible offspring genotype. [2 marks — 1 for purpose, 1 for method of construction.]

practice_questions.text: A woman is a carrier for cystic fibrosis (Ff). Her partner does not carry the allele (FF). Explain the probability that their child will have cystic fibrosis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cross Ff × FF. Gametes: F or f (mother); F (father). Offspring genotypes: FF and Ff in a 1:1 ratio. No offspring can be ff, so the probability of cystic fibrosis is 0%. The father has no f allele to pass on, so the recessive phenotype cannot appear.
Secure: Punnett square shown; correct offspring genotypes; probability stated as 0% with reason.
Developing: States the child cannot have cystic fibrosis, but reasoning is incomplete.
Emerging: States one parent is a carrier but does not complete the cross.

practice_questions.text: Both parents are carriers of cystic fibrosis (Ff). They have four children. Suggest why it is possible that none of their children have cystic fibrosis, even though the predicted ratio is 3 unaffected : 1 affected.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The Punnett square gives probabilities (25% per child) based on the laws of chance. With only four children, it is entirely possible — though unlikely — for no child to inherit the ff genotype. Each pregnancy is an independent event; previous outcomes have no effect on the next. With small sample sizes, actual results often deviate significantly from predicted ratios.
Secure: Probabilities are independent per child; small sample sizes cause deviation from predicted ratios.
Developing: Probability doesn't guarantee the outcome; random chance.
Emerging: They might just be lucky.

practice_questions.text: Compare the pattern of inheritance of cystic fibrosis (recessive) with polydactyly (dominant) in a family pedigree.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cystic fibrosis can skip generations because carriers (Ff) appear unaffected; two unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child. Polydactyly appears in every generation because only one copy of the dominant allele is needed; an affected individual has a 50% chance of passing it to each child if heterozygous. In a pedigree, recessive conditions appear sporadically; dominant conditions appear in every generation.
Secure: Cystic fibrosis skips generations; polydactyly appears in every generation; explanation linked to dominant/recessive allele behaviour.
Developing: One condition can skip generations; the other can't; some reason given.
Emerging: One is dominant, one is recessive.

practice_questions.text: A couple want to know whether future children could be affected by a genetic condition that runs in one partner's family. Evaluate the usefulness of genetic testing and Punnett square analysis in advising this couple.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Genetic testing can identify whether each partner carries a relevant allele, providing actual genotype data rather than family history estimates. Punnett square analysis can then calculate precise probabilities for each pregnancy outcome. Limitations: probability does not guarantee outcome; genetic testing is not always available for all conditions; results may cause anxiety or affect insurance/employment; some conditions are polygenic and cannot be predicted from a single gene test. A balanced conclusion notes that combined testing and counselling gives the most informed picture, while recognising uncertainty remains.
Secure: Benefits of testing (confirms genotype, allows probability calculation) and limitations (probabilistic only, ethical/emotional impact) addressed clearly.
Developing: Some benefits listed; one limitation mentioned.
Emerging: Testing is useful but might be worrying.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the albedo of a surface.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface [accept: the fraction of incident radiation reflected back to space].

practice_questions.text: Describe the greenhouse effect and explain how it keeps Earth’s surface warmer than it would otherwise be.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Earth’s surface emits infrared radiation; greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb this and re-emit some back towards the surface. 1 mark: this reduces the amount of energy lost to space, so the surface reaches a higher equilibrium temperature than it would without greenhouse gases.

practice_questions.text: Explain why melting Arctic sea ice is considered a positive feedback in climate change.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: ice has a high albedo so reflects a large fraction of incoming solar radiation. 1 mark: when ice melts, it is replaced by darker ocean water which has a lower albedo. 1 mark: more solar radiation is absorbed by the ocean surface, causing further warming, which melts more ice — the process amplifies itself.

practice_questions.text: A student claims that because scientists disagree about the exact amount of future warming, there is no reliable scientific basis for climate concern. Evaluate this claim using your understanding of scientific models and evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (4): distinguishes between uncertainty about magnitude/timing (where models genuinely disagree) and the underlying physics (which is well-established and agreed); explains that multiple independent lines of evidence (isotopic data, ice cores, stratospheric cooling pattern) all point to human-caused warming; notes that uncertainty in prediction does not mean equal likelihood of all outcomes; reaches a justified conclusion that the claim misrepresents how scientific uncertainty works.
Secure (3): identifies that models disagree on detail but the basic mechanism is agreed; gives one or two lines of evidence.
Developing (2): correctly identifies that some evidence exists but does not evaluate the uncertainty claim.
Emerging (1): makes one relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the atmosphere absorbs outgoing infrared radiation but allows most incoming visible light to pass through to Earth’s surface.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: greenhouse gas molecules (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O) have vibrational modes at infrared wavelengths, so they absorb infrared. 1 mark: the main atmospheric gases (N₂ and O₂) do not absorb visible light, so it passes through to the surface. 1 mark: outgoing infrared is selectively absorbed by the greenhouse gases — creating the asymmetry that drives the greenhouse effect.

practice_questions.text: A report states that switching from coal-fired power stations to solar panels will slow climate change. Evaluate this claim using your understanding of the physics of the greenhouse effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): explains that coal burning releases CO₂ by combustion of fossil carbon; links increased atmospheric CO₂ to enhanced infrared absorption and disrupted energy balance; explains that solar panels generate electricity without CO₂ emissions during operation; reasons that lower emission rates slow the rate at which CO₂ accumulates; acknowledges that existing CO₂ remains in the atmosphere for a long time so temperature continues rising until a new equilibrium; notes that energy balance is a physical law — reducing the rate of imbalance slows warming but does not immediately reverse it. Reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure (3–4): covers the physical mechanism and the role of emissions with partial evaluation.
Developing (2): identifies that coal emits CO₂ and solar does not, with limited physical explanation.
Emerging (1): makes one relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Name the non-metal in the reactivity series that is used as a reference point for acid reactions.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: hydrogen. Developing: gives a metal name instead. Emerging: no answer.

practice_questions.text: Describe what you would observe when iron is placed into copper sulfate solution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the blue solution turns pale green AND a brown/reddish solid (copper) is deposited on the iron. Secure: blue to pale green, brown solid forms. Developing: mentions colour change only. Emerging: vague change described.

practice_questions.text: Explain why zinc can be extracted from zinc oxide using carbon, but aluminium cannot be extracted from aluminium oxide in the same way.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: carbon is above zinc but below aluminium in the reactivity series; carbon is more reactive than zinc so it can displace zinc from its oxide (reducing it); carbon is less reactive than aluminium so it cannot displace aluminium from its oxide. Secure: carbon above zinc so can reduce zinc oxide; carbon below aluminium so cannot reduce aluminium oxide. Developing: mentions reactivity without explanation. Emerging: describes extraction without reference to relative reactivity.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Compare phytoextraction and conventional carbon reduction as methods for extracting metals. Suggest when each method would be more appropriate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: carbon reduction is fast, produces large quantities, used for reactive metals below carbon; phytoextraction is slow, used for low-grade ores, lower energy and environmental impact, more sustainable for small scale or where ore grades are too low for conventional mining. Secure: speed/scale difference noted and one advantage of each. Developing: describes one method accurately. Emerging: names the methods without comparison.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A manufacturing company needs to produce 500 tonnes of aluminium per year. It is considering whether to use conventional electrolysis or a newly developed bioleaching process. Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each method and reach a justified conclusion about which to recommend.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: electrolysis advantages (fast, large scale, established); disadvantages (very high energy cost, expensive, environmental cost of electricity generation); bioleaching advantages (lower energy, can use low-grade ores, more sustainable); disadvantages (slow, does not produce large quantities quickly); justified conclusion referencing 500 tonne target and speed of production, favouring electrolysis for this scale but acknowledging environmental trade-off. Secure: clear advantages and disadvantages for both with a justified conclusion. Developing: advantages and disadvantages for one method, partial conclusion. Emerging: names both methods without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why magnesium is more reactive than copper.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: magnesium loses its two outer electrons much more easily than copper does; magnesium therefore forms Mg²⁺ ions readily, while copper holds its outer electrons tightly and forms ions far less readily; the easier the electron loss, the more reactive the metal. Secure: magnesium loses electrons more easily to form positive ions. Developing: magnesium is higher in the reactivity series with some attempt at an electron reason. Emerging: magnesium is more reactive without explanation.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between speed and velocity.
practice_questions.marks: Speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only); velocity is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the gradient of a velocity-time graph represents and what it means when the gradient is negative.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: States that gradient represents acceleration.
Secure: The gradient of a velocity-time graph equals the acceleration (1 mark); a negative gradient means the object is decelerating — its velocity is decreasing over time (1 mark). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A delivery van travels at 20 m/s. The driver applies the brakes and the van decelerates uniformly to rest in 8 seconds. Calculate the deceleration of the van.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Selects the correct equation a = (v - u) / t.
Developing: Substitutes values correctly: a = (0 - 20) / 8 (1 mark).
Secure: Calculates: a = -2.5 m/s² (1 mark). States that the negative sign indicates deceleration (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A distance-time graph for a journey shows a horizontal section followed by a steeply rising straight line, then a gently rising straight line, and finally a return to the original distance value. Describe the motion shown in each section and compare the speed in the second and third sections.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Correctly describes one section (e.g. horizontal = stationary).
Secure: Horizontal = stationary (1 mark); steeply rising straight line = fast constant speed (1 mark); gently rising straight line = slower constant speed (1 mark).
Mastering: Correctly states that the second section has a greater speed than the third because its gradient is steeper; final section returning to original distance would require moving in the opposite direction (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 25 m/s in 10 s, then immediately brakes uniformly and stops in 5 s. Sketch the shape of the velocity-time graph. Calculate the acceleration during the first 10 s and the deceleration during the last 5 s. Suggest what would be different about the graph if the road surface were wet and braking took twice as long.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Correct overall shape described or sketched (straight line up, straight line down) (1 mark).
Secure: Acceleration = (25-0)/10 = 2.5 m/s² (1 mark). Deceleration = (0-25)/5 = -5 m/s² (1 mark).
Mastering: On a wet road, braking takes 10 s; the deceleration gradient is shallower (-2.5 m/s² instead of -5 m/s²), and the area under the braking section (distance to stop) is greater — demonstrating why wet roads increase stopping distances (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Speed cameras monitor road safety. Evaluate how the physics of motion can be used to determine whether a driver was speeding and whether they were driving safely, beyond just measuring speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: States that speed cameras measure speed using distance and time.
Developing: Explains that average speed = distance/time; average speed cameras measure the time to travel a known distance between two points (1 mark). Identifies that instantaneous speed cameras use a shorter time interval to give speed at a specific moment (1 mark).
Secure: Considers acceleration — a car that is accelerating rapidly may be safe at its current speed but dangerous if it continues (1 mark). Discusses stopping distances — safe driving depends on keeping enough distance to stop given the reaction distance (constant speed phase) and braking distance (deceleration phase), both of which depend on speed (1 mark).
Mastering: Evaluates the limitations — speed cameras capture a snapshot in time and may miss dangerous accelerations or tailgating; physics suggests that speed alone is insufficient — safe driving depends on speed relative to conditions (road surface, visibility, traffic) (1 mark). Reaches a reasoned conclusion about what additional data (e.g. acceleration profiles, inter-vehicle distance) would give a fuller picture of safety (1 mark). [6 marks — levels marked]

practice_questions.text: State what happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an endothermic reaction.
practice_questions.marks: The temperature of the surroundings decreases / falls. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a student could use a polystyrene cup and thermometer to determine whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Measure and record the starting temperature of the reactants (1); carry out the reaction in the polystyrene cup and record the maximum or minimum temperature reached; if temperature rises, exothermic; if falls, endothermic (1).
Secure: Record temperature before and after; compare to determine direction of energy change (2).
Developing: Take temperature readings (1).
Emerging: Vague (0).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the activation energy is always shown as an upward arrow on a reaction profile, even in an exothermic reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Reactant particles must collide with sufficient energy to break bonds and begin the reaction (1); this always requires an input of energy, even if the overall reaction releases more energy than it absorbs (1); so the reaction profile must rise to a peak before the products form, regardless of whether the overall energy change is positive or negative (1).
Secure: Particles need minimum energy to react; activation energy is always an energy input (2).
Developing: States activation energy is required (1).
Emerging: Vague (0).

practice_questions.text: Compare the reaction profiles of an exothermic and an endothermic reaction. Refer to the relative energy levels of reactants and products and the activation energy in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Exothermic — products at lower energy level than reactants; overall energy change is negative (energy released) (1); Endothermic — products at higher energy level than reactants; overall energy change is positive (energy absorbed) (1); both have an activation energy barrier (peak above reactant level) (1); both show activation energy as the energy difference from reactant level to the peak of the profile (1).
Secure: Correct description of both profiles with reference to activation energy (2–3).
Developing: Correctly describes one profile (1).
Emerging: Confused (0).

practice_questions.text: A student uses a polystyrene cup to measure the temperature change when magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. The solution (50 g) rises from 20°C to 41°C. Using Q = mcΔT (c = 4.18 J/g/°C), calculate the energy released. Suggest one improvement to make the result more accurate and explain why this improvement helps.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: ΔT = 41 − 20 = 21°C (1); Q = 50 × 4.18 × 21 = 4389 J = 4.39 kJ (1); Improvement: use a lid on the cup to reduce heat loss to the air (1); because this reduces the temperature drop during the experiment, giving a result closer to the actual heat released (1).
Secure: Correct calculation and one improvement with reason (2–3).
Developing: Correct calculation only (1–2).
Emerging: Incorrect or vague (0).

practice_questions.text:
(Higher tier) Using bond energies, calculate the overall energy change for the following reaction and state whether it is exothermic or endothermic. 
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
Bond energies: N≡N = 945 kJ/mol; H–H = 436 kJ/mol; N–H = 391 kJ/mol.
Show all your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Bonds broken: 1 × N≡N = 945; 3 × H–H = 3 × 436 = 1308; total breaking = 945 + 1308 = 2253 kJ/mol (1+1). Bonds made: 2 × 3 × N–H = 6 × 391 = 2346 kJ/mol (1+1). Energy change = 2253 − 2346 = −93 kJ/mol (1). Negative answer → exothermic; energy is released to the surroundings (1).
Secure: Correct method and most arithmetic correct (4–5).
Developing: Correct identification of bonds broken and made but arithmetic errors (2–3).
Emerging: Some bonds identified (1).

practice_questions.text: Balance the following equation: __ Mg + __ O<sub>2</sub> → __ MgO
practice_questions.marks: Award: 2Mg + O<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO. Coefficients 2, 1, 2 or equivalent correct balanced equation.

practice_questions.text: Write the formula of calcium chloride, given that calcium forms Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions and chloride is Cl<sup>−</sup>.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: CaCl<sub>2</sub> written correctly (1) with explanation that 2 chloride ions balance the 2+ charge (1).
Secure: correct formula, no explanation.
Developing: attempts to balance charges but formula incorrect.
Emerging: formula given without reference to charges.

practice_questions.text: The equation for the decomposition of copper carbonate is: CuCO<sub>3</sub> → CuO + CO<sub>2</sub>. If 62 g of CuCO<sub>3</sub> decomposes, calculate the mass of CuO produced. (M<sub>r</sub>: CuCO<sub>3</sub> = 124, CuO = 80.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: moles of CuCO<sub>3</sub> = 62 ÷ 124 = 0.5 mol (1); mole ratio 1:1 so 0.5 mol CuO (1); mass = 0.5 × 80 = 40 g (1).
Secure: method correct, arithmetic error in one step.
Developing: moles calculated but ratio step missing.
Emerging: formula correct but no mole calculation.

practice_questions.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia: \(N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3\). Compare the mass of ammonia produced from 28 g of nitrogen versus 6 g of hydrogen (assume the other reactant is in excess). (M<sub>r</sub>: N<sub>2</sub> = 28, H<sub>2</sub> = 2, NH<sub>3</sub> = 17.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: from N<sub>2</sub>: moles = 28 ÷ 28 = 1 mol; ratio 1:2 so 2 mol NH<sub>3</sub>; mass = 34 g (2); from H<sub>2</sub>: moles = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 mol; ratio 3:2 so 2 mol NH<sub>3</sub>; mass = 34 g (2); both give 34 g — comparison stated.
Secure: both calculations correct, comparison not explicitly stated.
Developing: one calculation correct.
Emerging: moles calculated for one substance only.

practice_questions.text: Iron reacts with sulfuric acid according to: Fe + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → FeSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. Calculate the mass of hydrogen gas produced from 0.4 mol of iron, and give the state symbols for all four substances. (M<sub>r</sub> of H<sub>2</sub> = 2.)
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mole ratio Fe:H<sub>2</sub> = 1:1 so 0.4 mol H<sub>2</sub> (1); mass = 0.4 × 2 = 0.8 g (1); correct state symbols Fe(s), H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq), FeSO<sub>4</sub>(aq), H<sub>2</sub>(g) (1).
Secure: mass correct, some state symbols wrong.
Developing: mass correct, state symbols not attempted.
Emerging: ratio identified but calculation incomplete.

practice_questions.text: A student is asked to balance and use the equation for the complete combustion of propane: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O. First balance the equation. Then calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 22 g of propane burns completely. (M<sub>r</sub>: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> = 44, CO<sub>2</sub> = 44.) Explain each step of your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: balanced equation \(C_3H_8 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 3CO_2 + 4H_2O\) (2); moles propane = 22 ÷ 44 = 0.5 mol (1); ratio 1:3 so 1.5 mol CO<sub>2</sub> (1); mass = 1.5 × 44 = 66 g (1); each step clearly explained (1).
Secure: balanced equation and mass correct, limited explanation of steps.
Developing: equation balanced but ratio applied incorrectly.
Emerging: equation partially balanced, mass calculation not reached.

practice_questions.text: Name the organelle that is the site of aerobic respiration.
practice_questions.marks: Mitochondria (accept mitochondrion). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two differences between a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Prokaryotic cells lack a true nucleus — their DNA is a single loop free in the cytoplasm — whereas eukaryotic cells have a nucleus enclosed by a membrane. Prokaryotic cells are typically much smaller than eukaryotic cells (and lack membrane-bound organelles).
Secure: Two clear structural differences stated.
Developing: One difference stated correctly.
Emerging: A general statement that they are different types of cell.

practice_questions.text: A student observes a cell under the electron microscope and sees folded inner membranes inside an organelle. Explain what this suggests about the function of that organelle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The folded inner membranes (cristae) greatly increase the surface area available for respiration enzymes. This suggests the organelle is a mitochondrion and that the cell carries out a high rate of aerobic respiration. Greater surface area means more enzyme active sites, so more reactions can occur simultaneously, increasing the rate of ATP production.
Secure: Folded membranes increase surface area; this is a mitochondrion involved in aerobic respiration.
Developing: Mitochondrion — used for respiration.
Emerging: The cell is active.

practice_questions.text: A cell drawn in a textbook measures 30 mm in diameter. The real cell is 0.02 mm in diameter. Calculate the magnification. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnification = image size ÷ real size = 30 mm ÷ 0.02 mm = ×1500. Both sizes in the same unit (mm), correct formula applied, correct answer with × symbol.
Secure: Correct formula and correct answer ×1500.
Developing: Correct formula but arithmetic error, or correct answer without showing working.
Emerging: Attempt to calculate with formula shown.

practice_questions.text: Suggest why electron microscopes rather than light microscopes were needed to discover the internal structure of mitochondria.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Mitochondrial internal structures (cristae, inner membrane folds) are measured in nanometres. The resolution of a light microscope is around 200 nm — insufficient to distinguish features this small. The electron microscope has a resolution of around 0.2 nm, around 1,000 times better, allowing structures of nanometre scale to be seen as separate objects. Without this resolution, the cristae would appear as a blurred mass within the mitochondrion.
Secure: Light microscope resolution too low; electron microscope resolution high enough to distinguish nanometre-scale features.
Developing: Electron microscopes magnify more.
Emerging: Electron microscopes are better.

practice_questions.text: The development of the electron microscope has been described as a major advance in scientific understanding of cells. Evaluate this claim, with reference to specific discoveries it enabled.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Prior to electron microscopy, scientists could observe cells and nuclei with light microscopes but could not resolve internal organelle structure. The electron microscope (TEM) revealed the cristae of mitochondria — folded inner membranes that increase the surface area for respiration enzymes — explaining why mitochondria are efficient at ATP production. It also resolved ribosome structure and the double membrane of the nucleus. These discoveries confirmed and refined the cell theory model. However, electron microscopes cannot be used on living specimens (the preparation process kills cells), and the images require interpretation. So while the electron microscope enormously advanced structural biology, it has limitations for studying dynamic processes in living cells.
Secure: Two specific discoveries named and explained; evaluation includes at least one limitation.
Developing: One discovery and one limitation.
Emerging: General statement that electron microscopes show more detail.

before.exam_tip_html: Magnification calculations are reliably examined. The most common mistake is using different units for image size and real size — always convert to the same unit first. When asked to ‘explain’ how microscopy has improved our understanding of cells, the examiners want you to use causal language: state what the technology allowed scientists to see, then explain how this changed or extended the scientific explanation (model). Listing microscope types without linking them to specific discoveries will not score the highest marks.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'differentiation'.
practice_questions.marks: The process by which a cell becomes specialised in structure and function. [1 mark. Must convey specialisation — not just 'cells change'.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a red blood cell that make it well adapted to its function.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Biconcave shape increases surface area for oxygen absorption; no nucleus maximises space for haemoglobin, increasing oxygen-carrying capacity. Both features linked to function.
Secure: Two features each with function stated.
Developing: Two features named without linking to function.
Emerging: One feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain why embryonic stem cells are considered more useful for medical therapies than adult stem cells.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent — they can differentiate into any cell type in the body. Adult stem cells can only produce cells of their own tissue type (e.g. bone marrow stem cells only make blood cells). Because embryonic stem cells can become any tissue, they could in principle be used to replace cells damaged by a wider range of diseases.
Secure: Embryonic = any cell type (pluripotent); adult = limited range.
Developing: Embryonic stem cells can become more types of cells.
Emerging: Embryonic stem cells are more flexible.

practice_questions.text: A scientist argues that iPS cells should replace embryonic stem cells in all medical research. Suggest one reason that supports this view and one reason that challenges it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Support: iPS cells are made from a patient's own adult cells, avoiding the ethical issue of embryo destruction and reducing immune rejection risk. Challenge: iPS cell reprogramming is a complex and relatively new technique; the cells may not be as stable as embryonic stem cells, carrying a risk of uncontrolled division or incomplete differentiation. The long-term safety record for iPS cells is shorter than for embryonic stem cell research.
Secure: One clear point for and one against, with explanation.
Developing: One point for and one against, limited explanation.
Emerging: One point only.

practice_questions.text: A student says 'DNA doubles during mitosis.' Explain why this statement is incorrect and give the correct account of when DNA replication occurs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The statement is incorrect because DNA replication occurs during interphase, before mitosis begins — not during mitosis itself. During interphase, each chromosome is copied so that there are two identical copies. Mitosis then separates these copies into two new nuclei, producing two daughter cells each with the same DNA as the parent. By the time mitosis starts, the DNA has already been replicated.
Secure: DNA replication is before mitosis (during interphase); mitosis separates the copies.
Developing: DNA copies itself before mitosis.
Emerging: The replication happens before.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of embryonic stem cells in treating Parkinson's disease. Include scientific arguments and ethical considerations in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Scientific case for: embryonic stem cells are pluripotent and could be directed to differentiate into dopamine-producing neurones to replace those lost in Parkinson's disease, potentially restoring motor function. Risks include immune rejection and tumour formation if cells do not differentiate fully. Ethical case for: Parkinson's disease causes severe suffering; early embryos (3–5 days) have no consciousness. Ethical case against: using an embryo destroys a potential human life — those who believe life begins at fertilisation hold this is morally wrong. The decision cannot be made on science alone; it requires weighing evidence-based risks against values-based views on embryonic life.
Secure: Scientific argument with risks; one point for and one against ethically; acknowledgement that science and values are both involved.
Developing: Scientific argument; ethical argument; limited integration.
Emerging: Describes stem cells and mentions ethics without developing either.

before.exam_tip_html: In questions about stem cells and ethics, examiners want you to distinguish between scientific arguments (evidence about what stem cells can do, risks of rejection or tumour formation) and values-based arguments (beliefs about when human life begins, moral weight of potential cures). If you merge these, you lose marks. Always name the type of stem cell you are describing — ‘stem cell’ alone is insufficient. For the mitosis misconception: state clearly that DNA replication happens before mitosis, during interphase. Do not say DNA doubles ‘during mitosis’.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: in a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave the vibrations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer. [Accept either one distinction stated clearly.]

practice_questions.text: A water wave has a frequency of 2.5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.60 m. Calculate the wave speed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: correct substitution \(v = 2.5 \times 0.60\). 1 mark: \(v = 1.5 \text{ m/s}\) (with unit).

practice_questions.text: Explain why sound diffracts noticeably around a doorway but light does not.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: diffraction is greatest when the gap is similar in size to the wavelength. 1 mark: sound wavelengths (approximately 0.1–10 m) are comparable to the width of a doorway (approximately 1 m). 1 mark: visible light has a much shorter wavelength (approximately 400–700 nm), far smaller than a doorway, so very little diffraction occurs.

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of radio waves and gamma rays, explaining why one is used in medical treatment and the other in long-distance communication.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: both are electromagnetic waves travelling at the same speed in a vacuum. 1 mark: gamma rays have a much higher frequency (shorter wavelength) and carry more energy per photon — they are ionising and can destroy cancer cells (used in radiotherapy). 1 mark: radio waves have a low frequency, low energy, are not ionising, and travel through the atmosphere with little absorption — making them ideal for long-distance broadcasting. 1 mark: using gamma for communication would be hazardous to people and difficult to generate at scale; radio waves cannot ionise cells so are safe for widespread use.

practice_questions.text: A radar system uses microwaves with a frequency of \(10 \text{ GHz}\) (\(10 \times 10^9 \text{ Hz}\)). Calculate the wavelength of these microwaves. (Speed of EM waves in air \(= 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}\))
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: \(\lambda = \frac{v}{f} = \frac{3 \times 10^8}{10 \times 10^9}\). 1 mark: \(\lambda = 0.03 \text{ m}\) (3 cm) [with unit].

practice_questions.text: Ultraviolet radiation causes skin cancer but is also used to sterilise drinking water. Evaluate whether the use of UV in water treatment is justified, using your knowledge of how UV radiation interacts with living cells.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): explains that UV is ionising (damages DNA) and kills microorganisms; distinguishes between exposure of skin (where DNA in skin cells can be mutated) and exposure of water flowing through a UV steriliser (where microorganisms are killed without adding chemicals to the water); evaluates the scale of benefit (safe drinking water prevents disease in large populations) versus the risk (the public are not directly exposed to the UV; only operators need protective equipment); acknowledges that compared with chemical treatment (chlorine), UV leaves no residue and is therefore preferred in some systems; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure (3–4): identifies the benefit (kills microorganisms) and risk (ionising, can cause cancer) with partial evaluation.
Developing (2): states both UV kills bacteria and UV causes cancer but does not evaluate.
Emerging (1): one relevant point.
