practice_questions.text: State Newton's First Law of motion.
practice_questions.marks: An object remains at rest, or continues to move at constant velocity, unless acted upon by a resultant (unbalanced) force. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A driver travelling at 30 m/s sees a hazard ahead and brakes to a stop. Describe two factors, other than speed, that could increase the driver's braking distance.
practice_questions.marks: Any two of: wet or icy road surface; worn tyres (reduced grip); worn or overheated brakes; heavily loaded vehicle (greater mass increases stopping distance). [1 mark each, max 2]

practice_questions.text: A 900 kg car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 8 seconds. The driving force is 3 000 N. Calculate the resultant force acting on the car and explain what the difference between driving force and resultant force tells you about other forces acting.
practice_questions.marks: Acceleration = (20 − 0) ÷ 8 = 2.5 m/s² [1 mark]. Resultant force = 900 × 2.5 = 2 250 N [1 mark]. The resultant force (2 250 N) is less than the driving force (3 000 N), so friction and air resistance together must be 750 N opposing motion [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A car of mass 1 400 kg is travelling at 15 m/s when it collides with a stationary car of mass 1 000 kg. The two cars stick together after the collision. Calculate the velocity of the combined cars immediately after the collision, and suggest why the actual velocity might be slightly less than your calculated value.
practice_questions.marks: Momentum before = 1400 × 15 = 21 000 kg m/s [1 mark]. Combined mass = 2 400 kg [1 mark]. Velocity = 21 000 ÷ 2 400 = 8.75 m/s [1 mark]. Actual velocity may be slightly less because friction from the road acts on the cars during the impact, so the system is not perfectly closed. Kinetic energy is also transferred to sound, heating and deformation of the metal, but that does not by itself reduce momentum [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A road safety campaign claims that 'doubling your speed more than doubles your stopping distance.' Using your knowledge of kinetic energy and stopping distance, evaluate this claim. Consider both thinking distance and braking distance in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Thinking distance is proportional to speed (doubles when speed doubles) because the distance covered during reaction time = speed × reaction time. Braking distance depends on kinetic energy (KE = ½mv²), which is proportional to v² — so doubling speed quadruples KE and therefore braking distance. Overall stopping distance more than doubles because the braking component grows disproportionately. The claim is correct — and the effect is even more significant at higher speeds (e.g. motorway). Evaluation: the claim understates the increase for the braking component. Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly identifies that braking distance grows faster than speed; gives partial equation support. Developing (1–2 marks): States that speed increases stopping distance but without quantitative reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using Newton's Third Law, why a rocket can accelerate in the vacuum of space where there is no air to push against.
practice_questions.marks: The rocket expels high-speed gases downward (action force on gases) [1 mark]. By Newton's Third Law, the gases exert an equal and opposite force on the rocket upward (reaction force on rocket) [1 mark]. Because these are forces on different objects (gases and rocket), the rocket experiences an upward resultant force and accelerates — no air or surface is needed to push against [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A current of 2 A flows through a circuit for 30 seconds. Calculate the total charge that passes a point in the circuit.
Describe how the current and potential difference behave differently in a series circuit compared with a parallel circuit.
practice_questions.marks: In a series circuit, current is the same at every point but the potential difference is shared (split) across the components [1 mark]. In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is the same as the supply, but the current splits between branches [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A 6 V battery is connected to three resistors in series: 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 2 Ω. Calculate the total resistance and the current in the circuit. Then calculate the potential difference across the 6 Ω resistor.
practice_questions.marks: Total resistance = 4 + 6 + 2 = 12 Ω [1 mark]. Current I = V ÷ R = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A [1 mark]. V across 6 Ω = 0.5 × 6 = 3 V [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Finds total resistance and current correctly but cannot calculate the pd across one resistor.

practice_questions.text: A lamp filament has a resistance of 240 Ω when hot. Calculate the current through the lamp when connected to a 12 V supply. Suggest why the resistance of the filament is much lower when the lamp is first switched on (before it heats up).
practice_questions.marks: I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 240 = 0.05 A [1 mark]. When first switched on, the filament is cold [1 mark], so its resistance is lower [1 mark] because resistance of a metal increases with temperature (hotter metal atoms vibrate more, impeding charge flow more) [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct current and explains that cold filament has lower resistance due to temperature.
Developing: Correct current but does not explain resistance change in terms of temperature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why adding a resistor in parallel to an existing resistor decreases the total resistance of the circuit, even though you are adding more resistance.
practice_questions.marks: Adding a parallel branch provides an additional path for charge to flow [1 mark]. More paths mean more charge can flow per second for the same potential difference [1 mark], which is equivalent to a lower total resistance (since higher current at the same voltage means lower resistance by V = IR) [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that parallel adds a path and reduces resistance but does not link to current or V = IR.

practice_questions.text: A circuit contains a thermistor in series with a fixed resistor and a battery. The temperature of the thermistor rises. Evaluate what happens to the current in the circuit and the potential difference across the fixed resistor. Support your answer with reasoning from the relevant equations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that thermistor resistance decreases as temperature rises (correct property). Uses V = IR to reason: total resistance decreases, so for the same battery voltage, total current I = V/R_total increases. Applies the voltage-divider logic: because the fixed resistor's resistance is unchanged but current increases, the pd across the fixed resistor (V = I × R_fixed) increases. The pd across the thermistor decreases. Presents a coherent chain of reasoning.
Secure: Identifies thermistor resistance falls, current rises, pd across fixed resistor increases with correct use of V = IR.
Developing: Correctly identifies that thermistor resistance falls and current rises but does not address the pd across the fixed resistor.
Emerging: States thermistor resistance falls without further correct reasoning.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by an exothermic reaction in terms of energy and temperature change.
practice_questions.marks: Award: a reaction in which energy is transferred to the surroundings, causing the temperature of the surroundings to rise. Accept equivalent correct wording.

practice_questions.text: In a bond energy calculation, what does a negative overall energy change tell you about the reaction?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: more energy is released making bonds than is required to break bonds (1), so the reaction is exothermic and transfers energy to surroundings (1).
Secure: states exothermic with partial explanation.
Developing: states exothermic but no explanation.
Emerging: incorrect interpretation of the sign.

practice_questions.text: The reaction of hydrogen with chlorine is: H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl. Bond energies: H–H = 436 kJ/mol; Cl–Cl = 243 kJ/mol; H–Cl = 432 kJ/mol. Calculate the overall energy change and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: energy in = 436 + 243 = 679 kJ (1); energy out = 2 × 432 = 864 kJ (1); ΔH = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ/mol, exothermic (1).
Secure: both totals correct, sign error or label missing.
Developing: one total correct, method partially shown.
Emerging: bond energies added without structure.

practice_questions.text: Sketch a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction and compare it with an endothermic reaction. On your diagram, label the activation energy and the overall energy change ΔH for each. Explain what activation energy represents.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: exothermic profile with products below reactants (1); endothermic profile with products above reactants (1); activation energy labelled as the peak above reactants for both (1); explanation that activation energy is the minimum energy for a reaction to occur (1).
Secure: both profiles sketched, one label missing.
Developing: one profile correct with activation energy labelled.
Emerging: one profile attempted.

practice_questions.text: The combustion of methane is: CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H = 413; O=O = 498; C=O = 805; O–H = 463. Calculate the overall energy change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: bonds broken = (4 × 413) + (2 × 498) = 1652 + 996 = 2648 kJ (1); bonds made = (2 × 805) + (4 × 463) = 1610 + 1852 = 3462 kJ (1); ΔH = 2648 − 3462 = −814 kJ/mol, exothermic (1).
Secure: method correct, one counting error.
Developing: bonds broken calculated correctly only.
Emerging: equation for ΔH stated but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A student claims that all reactions with a high activation energy must be exothermic. Evaluate this claim. In your answer, refer to reaction profiles and bond energy calculations and give an example that supports or contradicts the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: correctly states that activation energy and overall energy change are independent quantities (2); explains that endothermic reactions can also have high activation energies (2); uses reaction profile evidence with reference to the position of reactants and products relative to the peak (1); gives a valid example or argues the point with bond energy logic (1).
Secure: claim correctly refuted, profiles referenced, one element incomplete.
Developing: claim refuted with some reasoning, no profile reference.
Emerging: limited or confused response.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'random sample' in an ecological investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sample where every individual / location has an equal chance of being chosen, selected without bias (e.g. using random numbers / random coordinates).
Secure: Every location has an equal chance of being selected.
Developing: Reference to avoiding bias without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: A student records the number of earthworms in six 1 m² quadrats: 4, 7, 5, 6, 4, 8. Calculate the mean number of earthworms per quadrat. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sum = 4+7+5+6+4+8 = 34. Mean = 34 ÷ 6 = 5.67 (to 2 decimal places) or 5.7 earthworms per quadrat. (Both marks: correct sum and division shown [1] + correct answer [1].)
Secure: Method correct but arithmetic error in sum; or correct answer without working shown.
Developing: Addition attempted but division step missing or incorrect.
Emerging: One or two values summed with no clear method.

practice_questions.text: Using your answer from above, estimate the total number of earthworms in a 300 m² garden. The quadrats used are 1 m² each. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Number of quadrat-sized units in the garden = 300 ÷ 1 = 300. Estimated population = mean × 300 = 5.67 × 300 = 1,701 (or 5.7 × 300 = 1,710). (1 mark for method; 1 mark for correct calculation consistent with mean used.)
Secure: Correct method with minor arithmetic error; units used correctly.
Developing: Mean multiplied by 300 without justification; follow-through mark applied.
Emerging: Number of quadrats not considered.

practice_questions.text: In a woodland, the population of a bird species was 350 in Year 1. By Year 4, the population had risen to 427. Calculate the percentage change. Give your answer to one decimal place.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Percentage change = (427 − 350) ÷ 350 × 100 = 77 ÷ 350 × 100 = 22.0% increase. (3 marks: correct formula [1]; correct substitution and calculation [1]; correct rounding and unit/direction stated [1].)
Secure: Formula correct and calculation attempted; answer not rounded or direction not stated.
Developing: (427 − 350) calculated correctly but then divided by 427 (using new value); or formula not shown.
Emerging: Difference calculated (77) but no percentage conversion.

practice_questions.text: A student investigates dandelion abundance in a school field and a nearby car park. They use random quadrats in each location and record a mean of 12 dandelions per m² in the field and 2 per m² in the car park. Suggest two reasons why the number of dandelions is higher in the field.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two valid reasons with explanation, e.g.: (1) More light available in the field — fewer obstacles block sunlight, so dandelions can photosynthesise more effectively and grow more densely. (2) Greater soil depth and quality in the field — car park surfaces may have thin soil with fewer nutrients, reducing plant growth. (3) Less physical disturbance in the field — cars compacting car park ground may damage plants or make germination difficult. [2 marks per reason: 1 for suggestion, 1 for explanation using science.]
Secure: Two reasons suggested with partial explanation.
Developing: Two reasons stated without scientific explanation.
Emerging: One relevant reason stated.

practice_questions.text: A long-term study found that as the mean summer temperature increased in a region, the average abundance of a butterfly species in field surveys also increased. A researcher concludes that higher temperatures cause butterfly populations to increase. Evaluate this conclusion, referring to correlation, causation and alternative explanations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Evaluation uses both sides. Supporting the conclusion: the data shows a positive correlation between temperature and butterfly abundance; warmer temperatures may increase butterfly survival, extend the breeding season, or improve host plant growth, providing biological plausibility. Challenging the conclusion: correlation does not prove causation; a third variable (e.g. increased plant growth due to warmer, wetter summers) could explain both the temperature rise and the butterfly increase independently; without a controlled experiment, it is not possible to establish a causal link; other factors such as habitat management, pesticide reduction, or migration patterns could contribute to the increase. Quality of evidence: sample size, number of years, and consistency across sites affect reliability. Conclusion: the correlation is consistent with a causal link but does not prove it; further controlled investigation is needed. Uses evaluative language throughout.
Secure: Correlation vs causation addressed; some alternative explanations given; attempted conclusion.
Developing: Correlation noted but alternative explanations limited or absent; limited evaluation.
Emerging: One relevant point about correlation or causation with no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD)'.
practice_questions.marks: Testing embryos created by IVF for genetic conditions before implantation, so only unaffected embryos are selected. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between somatic gene therapy and germline gene therapy.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: Somatic gene therapy targets body cells of the patient and the changes are not inherited. Germline gene therapy targets reproductive cells or early embryos so changes would be passed on to future generations. [2 marks — 1 for each type correctly described.]

practice_questions.text: Explain why germline gene therapy is not currently permitted in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Changes to the germline would be inherited by future generations, so any unexpected harmful effects would be passed on; the long-term safety has not been established through evidence; this raises serious ethical concerns about making heritable changes to the human genome without the consent of future generations.
Secure: Germline changes are heritable; safety not established; ethical concerns about future generations.
Developing: It would affect children and is not safe yet.
Emerging: It is too risky.

practice_questions.text: A couple both carry the cystic fibrosis allele. Suggest two benefits and one risk of using PGD to select embryos free of the condition.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits — enables the couple to have biological children without fear of passing on a serious condition; prevents the suffering associated with cystic fibrosis in an affected child. Risk — IVF procedure itself carries medical risks for the woman; unused embryos carrying the faulty allele are destroyed, which raises ethical concerns for people who believe life begins at fertilisation.
Secure: Two clear benefits linked to the science; one risk with brief explanation.
Developing: Two benefits listed; risk noted briefly.
Emerging: PGD is useful; one vague benefit.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of GM crops to address vitamin A deficiency in countries where rice is the main food source.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Golden Rice produces beta-carotene in the grain; vitamin A deficiency causes blindness and immune problems in populations relying on rice; this is a clear, scientifically grounded benefit. However, risks include possible gene spread to wild relatives creating ecological problems; questions about whether dietary change or supplement programmes might address the deficiency with fewer risks; concerns about seed patent control by large corporations limiting farmer independence. Peer-reviewed evidence generally supports the safety of specific approved GM crops, but ‘safe’ is not the same as ‘beneficial for all’ — distributional and agricultural impacts also matter. A balanced conclusion weighs evidence and values.
Secure: Benefits (addresses nutritional deficiency) and risks (ecological, economic, ethical) developed with some evidence or reasoning.
Developing: Some benefits and risks listed without much development.
Emerging: States the crop helps but also has risks, little science used.

practice_questions.text: A 30-year-old individual tests positive for a genetic variant strongly associated with developing a serious condition later in life. Discuss the potential benefits and drawbacks of the individual having undergone this predictive genetic test.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits — knowledge allows the individual to seek regular monitoring, make lifestyle changes to reduce environmental risk factors, or plan their life (career, family, finances) accordingly; their close relatives could be offered testing. Drawbacks — psychological impact of knowing about a likely future condition can cause significant anxiety or depression; may affect insurance premiums or employment if the information becomes known; a positive test does not guarantee the condition will develop (especially if polygenic or environmentally influenced), so the test result may be misinterpreted. Conclusion weighs informed autonomy against psychological and practical harms.
Secure: Two or more benefits and two or more drawbacks developed, some linked to science.
Developing: Lists benefits and drawbacks without much development.
Emerging: States testing has pros and cons.

practice_questions.text: State one greenhouse gas other than carbon dioxide and give one human activity that produces it.
practice_questions.marks: Accept any of: methane from livestock farming / landfill / rice paddies; water vapour; nitrous oxide from agriculture. Both the gas and a valid source are needed. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the greenhouse effect warms the Earth’s surface.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly describes sunlight passing through the atmosphere, surface absorbing it and emitting infrared, greenhouse gases absorbing and re-emitting infrared back towards Earth, and the warming consequence.
Secure: Two of the above steps described accurately.
Developing: One correct step, e.g. ‘greenhouse gases trap heat’.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect description.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ice core data is considered strong evidence for the relationship between greenhouse gas concentrations and global temperatures.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that ice cores contain trapped air bubbles that directly preserve ancient atmospheric composition; that temperature can be reconstructed from isotope ratios in the same ice; that the two variables can therefore be compared directly over a very long time period; and that the data shows consistent correlation.
Secure: Two of the above points with causal language.
Developing: States that ice cores show CO₂ levels without explaining how or why this is strong evidence.
Emerging: Ice cores mentioned without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A student says: ‘Climate models are too uncertain to be useful.’ Evaluate this claim using your understanding of how scientific models work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that models involve simplifications and assumptions (source of uncertainty); but that models are tested against historical climate data; that agreement among independent modelling teams increases confidence; and that uncertainty about exact magnitude does not undermine confidence in the direction and cause of change.
Secure: Identifies both a limitation and a strength of models, with explanation.
Developing: Identifies either a strength or limitation but not both.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how scientists distinguish between natural climate variation and human-caused climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes that climate models are run with natural factors only (solar variation, volcanic eruptions) and the results compared with observed warming; that natural-factor-only models cannot reproduce the observed warming trend; that only when human greenhouse gas emissions are included do models match the data; concludes this is evidence of human causation.
Secure: Two of the above points.
Developing: States that natural factors exist but does not explain the modelling approach.
Emerging: States that humans cause climate change without explaining the reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A government adviser argues that because scientists disagree about exactly how much temperatures will rise by 2100, no action needs to be taken on greenhouse gas emissions. Evaluate this argument, using your scientific knowledge and understanding of evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Distinguishes clearly between well-established facts (rising temperatures, rising CO₂, human causation supported by mechanism and evidence) and genuine uncertainties (exact magnitude, regional effects, timing); explains that uncertainty about degree does not undermine the fundamental causal link; applies risk-benefit reasoning (acting reduces worst-case risk even under uncertainty); references specific evidence (ice cores, temperature records, modelling); reaches a justified, balanced conclusion.
Secure: Addresses both established evidence and uncertainty with mostly accurate science; some evaluative language; conclusion reached.
Developing: Lists some evidence but does not properly evaluate the adviser’s argument; limited distinction between certain and uncertain aspects.
Emerging: Simple or one-sided response; minimal use of evidence.

practice_questions.text: Name the electrode at which oxidation occurs during electrolysis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: anode. Developing: cathode. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to a cation when it reaches the cathode during electrolysis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the cation gains electrons at the cathode and is reduced to a neutral atom or molecule. Secure: gains electrons and becomes neutral. Developing: becomes a neutral atom. Emerging: moves to cathode.

practice_questions.text: Explain why copper is deposited at the cathode rather than hydrogen gas being produced when aqueous copper sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: both Cu²⁺ and H⁺ ions from water are present at the cathode; copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so Cu²⁺ ions are more easily discharged than H⁺; therefore copper metal is deposited in preference to hydrogen. Secure: copper below hydrogen in reactivity series, so copper discharged first. Developing: copper is less reactive. Emerging: copper goes to cathode.

practice_questions.text: Compare the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride with the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride solution. Explain how the products at the cathode differ and why.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: molten NaCl — only Na⁺ and Cl⁻ present, so sodium metal produced at cathode; aqueous NaCl — Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ present; sodium is above hydrogen in reactivity series so H⁺ ions are discharged in preference, producing hydrogen gas. Secure: identifies difference (Na vs H₂) and gives reactivity reason. Developing: names different products. Emerging: gives product for one condition only.

practice_questions.text: Aluminium is one of the most widely used metals in the world, yet its production by electrolysis is very expensive. Evaluate the factors that contribute to the high cost of aluminium production, and suggest why we should still invest in recycling aluminium rather than extracting it from ore.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: factors (aluminium above carbon so electrolysis required; high temperature to melt aluminium oxide; large electricity input; carbon electrodes burn away and must be replaced); recycling arguments (uses far less energy than extraction from ore; conserves finite bauxite reserves; reduces environmental impact of mining; economically viable despite collection costs). Secure: three cost factors identified and two recycling advantages with explanation. Developing: two factors identified, recycling mentioned. Emerging: electrolysis is expensive, recycling is better — without reasons.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode when molten lead bromide (PbBr₂) is electrolysed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Pb²⁺(l) + 2e⁻ → Pb(l) — correctly balanced charge and atoms, reduction identified. Secure: correct formula, correct electrons, minor error. Developing: direction of electrons correct but equation unbalanced. Emerging: identifies lead at cathode without equation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by active transport.
practice_questions.marks: The movement of substances from a lower to a higher concentration (against the concentration gradient), requiring energy from respiration. [1 mark. Must include 'against the gradient' and energy. Do not accept 'osmosis'.]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the structure of alveoli is adapted for efficient gas exchange.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Alveoli have walls that are one cell thick (short diffusion distance) and are surrounded by a dense network of capillaries that maintain a steep concentration gradient for oxygen and carbon dioxide. The large number of alveoli provides a very large total surface area.
Secure: Large surface area; thin walls; good blood supply (two of three for 2 marks).
Developing: Thin walls and large surface area named without full explanation.
Emerging: One feature named.

practice_questions.text: Explain why root hair cells use active transport to absorb nitrate ions from the soil, rather than diffusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The concentration of nitrate ions inside the root hair cell is already higher than in the soil water. Diffusion cannot move substances against their concentration gradient. Active transport uses energy (ATP from respiration) to move nitrate ions from the lower concentration in the soil to the higher concentration inside the cell, against the gradient.
Secure: Concentration inside cell is already higher than soil; active transport moves against gradient using energy.
Developing: Active transport moves against the gradient using energy.
Emerging: Active transport uses energy.

practice_questions.text: A student calculates the surface area to volume ratio for a 5 cm cube. Calculate this ratio and explain what it suggests about how this organism would supply its cells with oxygen.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Surface area = 6 × 5² = 150 cm². Volume = 5³ = 125 cm³. SA:V = 150:125 = 1.2:1. This very low ratio means the surface area is small relative to volume. Simple diffusion across the surface could not supply enough oxygen to reach cells deep in the interior fast enough. The organism would need specialised exchange surfaces (e.g. lungs) and a circulatory system.
Secure: Correct SA:V calculation; explanation that diffusion alone is insufficient and transport systems are needed.
Developing: Correct calculation; simple statement that the ratio is low.
Emerging: Attempt at calculation.

practice_questions.text: Compare the structure and function of a capillary with that of an artery.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; they have thick, elastic, muscular walls to withstand this pressure and a relatively narrow lumen. Capillaries carry blood through tissues; their walls are only one cell thick, which enables efficient diffusion of substances between blood and surrounding tissues. Arteries do not allow direct exchange with tissues; capillaries are the site of all substance exchange.
Secure: Wall thickness and function contrasted for both vessels.
Developing: Arteries have thick walls; capillaries have thin walls — some functional link.
Emerging: Named one difference.

practice_questions.text: Patients with emphysema have difficulty absorbing enough oxygen from the air. Evaluate how the disease process explains their symptoms, and suggest why some patients use supplemental oxygen therapy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In emphysema, alveolar walls break down due to inflammation (often caused by smoking), merging small alveoli into larger but fewer spaces. This reduces total surface area for gas exchange. Less surface area means less oxygen can diffuse into the blood per breath. The steep concentration gradient is also harder to maintain as blood flow in damaged capillary networks is reduced. As a result, blood oxygen levels fall, causing breathlessness. Supplemental oxygen increases the concentration of oxygen in inhaled air, steepening the gradient and partially compensating for reduced surface area, so more oxygen diffuses per breath despite the structural damage. A complete cure requires restoring alveolar structure, which is not currently possible.
Secure: Mechanism of damage linked to surface area reduction; gradient and diffusion rate explained; supplemental oxygen logic explained.
Developing: Surface area reduced; less oxygen absorbed; supplemental oxygen helps.
Emerging: Emphysema damages lungs; less oxygen absorbed.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a feedstock in the chemical industry.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a raw material used as the starting point for making other chemical products. Secure: raw material for making other chemicals. Developing: starting material. Emerging: vague reference to industry.

practice_questions.text: Describe how crude oil is separated by fractional distillation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: crude oil is heated so it vaporises; the vapours rise up a fractionating column that is cooler at the top; different fractions condense at different heights depending on their boiling points and are collected. Secure: heated, different boiling points, condense at different heights. Developing: mentions boiling points. Emerging: heated and separated.

practice_questions.text: Explain why petrol, which has shorter hydrocarbon chains, condenses near the top of the fractionating column while bitumen remains as a liquid residue at the bottom.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: shorter chains have weaker intermolecular forces; less energy is needed to overcome them, so they have lower boiling points and remain as vapour higher up the cooler column, condensing near the top; bitumen has very long chains with much stronger intermolecular forces and a much higher boiling point, so it never fully vaporises and remains as residue at the base. Secure: shorter chains, weaker forces, lower boiling point — all three linked. Developing: shorter chains have lower boiling point. Emerging: shorter molecules go to the top.

practice_questions.text: A chemist cracks dodecane (C₁₂H₂₆) and obtains ethene (C₂H₄) as one product. Suggest what the other product is and write a balanced equation for the reaction.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: other product = decane (C₁₀H₂₂); balanced equation: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₁₀H₂₂ + C₂H₄; identifies decane as an alkane and ethene as an alkene. Secure: correct formula for both products, equation balanced. Developing: identifies products but equation unbalanced. Emerging: names one product.

practice_questions.text: Crude oil is used in huge quantities worldwide both as a fuel and as a chemical feedstock. Evaluate the sustainability of our current dependence on crude oil, and suggest what chemists can do to address the problems it creates.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: identifies crude oil as finite; current consumption rate not sustainable; consequences (depletion, price rises, loss of feedstock for future polymers/medicines); for fuels — development of renewable alternatives (hydrogen, biofuels, electric vehicles); for feedstock — development of bio-based polymers and recycling of existing polymers; societal cost–benefit decision (IaS4 framing). Secure: finite nature identified, two future alternatives with explanation, sustainability conclusion. Developing: finite nature and one alternative. Emerging: mentions crude oil running out.

practice_questions.text: Explain what cracking is and why it is economically important for the petrochemical industry.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: cracking breaks down long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful molecules using heat and a catalyst or steam; it is economically important because demand for shorter-chain fuels (petrol) and alkenes (for polymers) is greater than supply from distillation alone, so cracking converts surplus heavier fractions into higher-value products. Secure: defines cracking and gives one economic reason. Developing: describes cracking process. Emerging: cracking splits molecules.

practice_questions.text: Name the type of pathogen that causes malaria.
practice_questions.marks: Protist (Plasmodium). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the body prevents pathogens from entering internal tissues.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: Any two of — skin acts as a physical barrier preventing penetration; mucus traps pathogens in airways; cilia sweep mucus and pathogens out of airways; stomach acid (pH 1–2) kills pathogens in food/drink; lysozyme in tears/saliva destroys bacterial cell walls. [1 mark per correct defence with brief explanation, 2 marks total.]

practice_questions.text: Explain how viruses cause damage to the body when they infect a host.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Viruses invade host cells and use the cell's own machinery (ribosomes, enzymes) to make copies of themselves; when replication is complete the new virus particles burst out of the cell (lysis), destroying it; as large numbers of cells are killed the tissue stops functioning properly, causing the symptoms of disease.
Secure: Invade cells, replicate inside, burst out destroying the cell; cell death causes symptoms.
Developing: Viruses get inside cells and replicate, which kills them.
Emerging: Viruses damage cells.

practice_questions.text: Cholera outbreaks often follow natural disasters such as floods or earthquakes. Suggest why, using your knowledge of how cholera is transmitted.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Cholera is transmitted through water or food contaminated with faeces containing the cholera bacterium. Disasters damage water treatment infrastructure and sewage systems, causing human waste to contaminate drinking water supplies. People displaced into crowded camps may have limited access to clean water or sanitation facilities. Together these conditions allow rapid spread through a population that would not occur under normal water-treatment conditions.
Secure: Transmission via contaminated water; disasters damage water/sewage systems leading to spread.
Developing: Water gets contaminated after a disaster so people drink dirty water with cholera in it.
Emerging: Dirty water causes cholera to spread.

practice_questions.text: Compare how bacteria and viruses each cause symptoms of disease in a host.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Bacteria reproduce rapidly inside the body and release toxins — chemicals that damage cells and tissues at a distance from the bacteria themselves; the toxins cause specific symptoms (e.g. cholera toxin causes severe fluid loss). Viruses invade host cells directly, replicate using the host cell's machinery, and destroy the cell when they burst out (lysis); cell destruction causes tissue damage and symptoms. Key difference: bacteria cause harm primarily via toxins from outside cells; viruses cause harm by destroying cells from within.
Secure: Bacteria release toxins; viruses replicate inside and destroy cells; difference stated.
Developing: Bacteria make toxins; viruses kill cells.
Emerging: Both damage cells; bacteria use toxins.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the effectiveness of barrier defences as a method of preventing infection compared with vaccination.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Barrier defences (skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, lysozyme) are non-specific, continuous and require no immune activation; they prevent the vast majority of pathogens from entering the body at any time. Limitations: they can be breached (cuts, damaged cilia from smoking); they do not provide specific protection against any one pathogen. Vaccination provides specific, long-lasting immunity by priming the immune system with memory cells; far more effective than barriers once a pathogen has entered the body. Limitation: vaccination must be developed for each specific pathogen and requires population-level uptake for herd immunity to work. A balanced conclusion: barriers are essential frontline prevention; vaccination is the key tool for preventing specific diseases once barriers are insufficient.
Secure: Barrier defences explained and evaluated; vaccination mechanism and effectiveness evaluated; both limitations acknowledged.
Developing: Describes barriers and vaccines; some comparison made.
Emerging: Lists barriers; states vaccines work differently.

practice_questions.text: State the name of the process used to kill harmful microorganisms in drinking water.
practice_questions.marks: Sterilisation (accept chlorination; accept UV treatment; accept ozone treatment).

practice_questions.text: Describe how filtration is used in water treatment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes water being passed through beds of sand and gravel; explains that this removes suspended solid particles and debris, producing visually clear water.
Secure: States that filtration uses sand/gravel to remove solids.
Developing: Vague description of filtration without specifying what is removed.
Emerging: Confused with sterilisation or no accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain why chlorine is preferred over UV light for sterilising drinking water in large supply networks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that chlorine continues to kill bacteria as water travels through distribution pipes (residual effect); that UV light only acts at the point of treatment; therefore chlorine provides lasting protection that UV cannot.
Secure: Two of the above points with causal link.
Developing: States chlorine is effective but does not compare with UV.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect comparison.

practice_questions.text: A coastal town in a water-scarce region is considering building either a distillation plant or a reverse osmosis plant to produce potable water. Compare the two methods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains how both methods work (distillation — boiling and condensing; reverse osmosis — forcing water through a semi-permeable membrane); compares energy requirement (both high, distillation typically more so); notes both produce concentrated brine as a by-product; concludes with a justified recommendation acknowledging the trade-offs (e.g. reverse osmosis is lower energy cost but membranes need maintenance).
Secure: Describes both methods with at least two points of comparison.
Developing: Describes one method accurately; vague on the other.
Emerging: One method described with limited accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Explain how agricultural fertiliser run-off can cause fish in a river to die.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that excess nitrates/phosphates in the river cause rapid algal growth (eutrophication); the algae block sunlight, killing aquatic plants; when the algae die, bacteria decompose them using dissolved oxygen; this depletes oxygen in the water, causing fish to suffocate.
Secure: Covers algal growth and oxygen depletion with causal language.
Developing: States fertilisers cause algal growth but does not explain the oxygen-depletion mechanism.
Emerging: States that fertilisers are bad for rivers without mechanism.

practice_questions.text: A water company is designing a supply system for a small island community that has a freshwater stream. The stream contains suspended sediment and bacteria. Evaluate the options for supplying safe drinking water to the community.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that fresh water is available so desalination is not needed; describes a full treatment process (filtration to remove sediment, then sterilisation to kill bacteria); evaluates sterilisation options (chlorine — residual protection, inexpensive; UV — effective but no residual; ozone — effective but more costly and complex); discusses practical considerations such as ongoing supply of chemicals and energy for UV; reaches a justified conclusion about which approach is most suitable for a small island.
Secure: Correct treatment steps described with reasoning; two or more options considered.
Developing: Correct steps described but options not compared or evaluated.
Emerging: Some relevant knowledge but poorly structured or missing key steps.

practice_questions.text: State the equation for calculating mean rate of reaction when measuring gas volume.
practice_questions.marks: Award: mean rate = volume of gas produced (cm³) ÷ time (s). Accept equivalent with correct units.

practice_questions.text: A student dissolves 3.6 g of sodium chloride in 200 cm³ of water. Calculate the concentration of the solution in g/dm³.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: converts 200 cm³ to 0.2 dm³ (1), concentration = 3.6 ÷ 0.2 = 18 g/dm³ (1).
Secure: method correct, conversion error only.
Developing: correct equation but volume not converted.
Emerging: equation stated but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A reaction between zinc and sulfuric acid produces 60 cm³ of gas in 30 s, then the reaction stops. Calculate the mean rate over the entire reaction and explain why the rate decreased as the reaction continued.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: mean rate = 60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s (1); rate decreased because zinc (or acid) was used up, so there are fewer reactant particles and collision frequency decreases (2).
Secure: mean rate correct, explanation partial (mentions ‘less reactant’ without linking to collisions).
Developing: mean rate correct, no explanation.
Emerging: calculation attempted but significant error.

practice_questions.text: A rate-of-reaction graph shows the volume of gas produced over time for two experiments: one with acid concentration 1 mol/dm³ and one with 2 mol/dm³. Compare the gradients of the two curves at the start and suggest what you would see in the final volumes of gas collected.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: higher concentration has steeper initial gradient = faster rate at start (1); collision frequency increases at higher concentration (1); both experiments produce the same final volume of gas (1) because the amount of zinc (the solid) is the limiting reactant (1).
Secure: gradients compared correctly, final volume reasoning present.
Developing: gradients correct, final volume not explained.
Emerging: states one curve is steeper without explanation.

practice_questions.text: 0.4 mol of potassium hydroxide is dissolved to make 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 250 cm³ = 0.25 dm³ (1); concentration = 0.4 ÷ 0.25 = 1.6 mol/dm³ (1).
Secure: correct method, arithmetic error accepted.
Developing: correct division but dm³ conversion missing.
Emerging: equation recalled but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A chemist investigates how a catalyst affects the rate of a reaction. The uncatalysed reaction takes 120 s to produce 30 cm³ of gas; the catalysed reaction produces the same volume in 40 s. Calculate the mean rate for each reaction, compare the rates and explain, using collision theory and the concept of activation energy, why the catalyst increases the rate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: uncatalysed rate = 30 ÷ 120 = 0.25 cm³/s (1); catalysed rate = 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 cm³/s (1); catalyst increases rate threefold (1); catalyst provides alternative pathway with lower activation energy (1); more collisions now have sufficient energy to react (1); catalyst is unchanged at end of reaction (1).
Secure: both rates correct, activation energy reasoning present, one element missing.
Developing: one rate correct, catalyst effect described.
Emerging: rates attempted, activation energy not mentioned.

practice_questions.text: State the law of conservation of energy.
practice_questions.marks: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred from one store to another. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A crane lifts a 2 000 N load through a vertical height of 8 m. Calculate the work done by the crane.
practice_questions.marks: W = F × d [1 mark for equation or substitution]; W = 2 000 × 8 = 16 000 J (or 16 kJ) [1 mark for correct answer with unit].

practice_questions.text: A 70 kg skateboarder rolls down a ramp, starting from rest at a height of 3 m. Calculate the speed at the bottom of the ramp, assuming no energy is lost to friction.
practice_questions.marks: GPE at top = mgh = 70 × 10 × 3 = 2 100 J [1 mark]. At bottom, GPE = KE, so ½mv² = 2 100, giving v² = 2 × 2 100 ÷ 70 = 60 [1 mark]. v = √60 ≈ 7.7 m/s [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A car of mass 1 000 kg travels at 20 m/s. A lorry of mass 8 000 kg travels at 5 m/s. Compare the kinetic energies of the two vehicles and suggest which would be harder to bring to a stop, justifying your answer.
practice_questions.marks: KE of car = ½ × 1 000 × 20² = 200 000 J [1 mark]. KE of lorry = ½ × 8 000 × 5² = 100 000 J [1 mark]. The car has greater KE [1 mark]. The car would require more braking force to stop in the same distance — or a longer braking distance — because more energy must be transferred by the brakes [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A wind turbine generates 500 000 J of electrical energy from 1 250 000 J of wind energy in a given time period. Calculate the efficiency of the turbine. Evaluate whether this is a reasonable efficiency for a large-scale energy generation device, and describe two ways engineers could try to improve energy efficiency in the overall electricity supply system.
practice_questions.marks: Efficiency = 500 000 ÷ 1 250 000 = 0.4 = 40% [1 mark]. Mastering (5–6): 40% is typical for a large wind turbine (real turbines reach roughly 35–50%); any energy conversion loses some energy through friction in moving parts, air resistance and heating in the generator coils. Improvement methods evaluated: reducing friction in bearings via lubrication; using higher-voltage transmission lines to reduce resistance heating losses; improving generator coil efficiency. Conclusion evaluates trade-offs (cost vs benefit of each improvement). Secure (3–4): Correct efficiency calculation plus 2 improvement methods with partial reasoning. Developing (1–2): Correct efficiency calculation only.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a car travelling at 30 m/s needs a much greater braking force to stop in the same distance as a car travelling at 15 m/s.
practice_questions.marks: KE depends on v², so at 30 m/s the car has four times the kinetic energy of the car at 15 m/s [1 mark]. The brakes do work (W = F × d) to transfer this kinetic energy [1 mark]. If the stopping distance is the same, a four times larger braking force is needed to transfer four times the energy [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A toaster draws a current of 4 A from a 230 V supply. Calculate its power rating.
A charge of 500 C flows through a lamp with a potential difference of 12 V across it. Calculate the energy transferred to the lamp.
practice_questions.marks: E = Q × V = 500 × 12 = 6,000 J [1 mark]. The energy is transferred to the lamp, mostly as light and thermal energy [1 mark — accept any statement correctly identifying the transfer].

practice_questions.text: A 1.5 kW hair dryer is used for 20 minutes each day for 30 days. Electricity costs 28p per kWh. Calculate the total cost of running the hair dryer over this period.
practice_questions.marks: Time = 20 min × 30 = 600 min = 10 hours [1 mark]. Energy = 1.5 kW × 10 h = 15 kWh [1 mark]. Cost = 15 × 28p = 420p = £4.20 [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Correctly calculates energy in kWh but makes an error in the time conversion or the final cost.

practice_questions.text: A resistor has a resistance of 50 Ω and a current of 0.6 A flowing through it. Calculate the power dissipated by the resistor. Then explain why this power appears as heating of the surroundings.
practice_questions.marks: P = I²R = 0.6² × 50 = 0.36 × 50 = 18 W [2 marks — 1 for correct squaring, 1 for final value]. As charge flows through the resistor, the moving charges collide with atoms in the material [1 mark], transferring energy to the thermal store of the resistor and then to the surroundings [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Correct power and explains charge–atom collisions causing heating.
Developing: Correct power calculation but explanation of heating is 'energy is lost' without mechanistic detail.

practice_questions.text: A step-up transformer in a power station increases voltage from 25,000 V to 400,000 V. The current in the primary coil is 800 A. Calculate the current in the secondary (high-voltage) coil.
practice_questions.marks: Using V_p × I_p = V_s × I_s: 25,000 × 800 = 400,000 × I_s [1 mark]. I_s = (25,000 × 800) ÷ 400,000 = 20,000,000 ÷ 400,000 = 50 A [1 mark]. State units: 50 A [1 mark — award final mark only if correct calculation shown].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Sets up the transformer equation correctly but makes an arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that 'the most effective way to reduce household electricity bills is to switch off appliances when not in use.' Use the equations for power, energy and cost to support or challenge this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses E = P × t to show that both power rating AND time of use contribute to energy consumed. Supports by calculating examples: a 2 kW heater left on for an hour costs more than a 100 W bulb left on for the same time. Challenges by noting that high-power appliances (ovens, showers, tumble dryers) may dominate the bill; switching off a phone charger (typically very low power) has negligible effect compared to reducing use of high-power devices. Suggests that reducing usage time of high-power appliances is most effective, not simply switching off standby devices. Uses cost = E × price to evaluate in financial terms. Reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure: Correctly uses E = P × t; discusses at least two different power-rated appliances; addresses time of use.
Developing: Identifies that power and time both matter but does not use equations to quantify.
Emerging: Agrees with the claim without engaging with the physics.

practice_questions.text: State two renewable energy sources.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two correct renewables from: solar / wind / hydroelectric / tidal / geothermal / wave / biomass.

practice_questions.text: Describe two environmental advantages of using wind turbines instead of a coal-fired power station to generate electricity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two of: wind turbines produce no CO₂ during operation (reducing contribution to climate change); wind turbines produce no sulfur dioxide (reducing acid rain); wind is a renewable source that will not run out; no radioactive waste produced. [Must relate advantage clearly to a comparison with coal.]

practice_questions.text: A power station receives 500 MJ of chemical energy from fuel and produces 150 MJ of useful electrical energy. Explain what happens to the remaining energy and calculate the efficiency of the station.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: the remaining 350 MJ (500 − 150) is transferred as thermal energy / wasted heat to the surroundings / cooling water. 1 mark: correct substitution \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{150}{500} \times 100\%\). 1 mark: efficiency = 30%.

practice_questions.text: Compare the reliability of wind power and nuclear power as energy sources for a national electricity grid.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: nuclear provides reliable baseload (runs continuously, output not weather-dependent). 1 mark: wind is intermittent and only generates when wind blows at sufficient speed. 1 mark: nuclear can precisely match demand; wind requires backup capacity or energy storage for calm periods. 1 mark: in terms of CO₂, both are low-carbon during operation, but nuclear produces long-lived radioactive waste whereas wind does not.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at very high voltage rather than at the voltage at which it is generated.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: for a given power, higher voltage means lower current (\(P = IV\)). 1 mark: power lost in cables is proportional to the current squared (\(P = I^2 R\)). 1 mark: so using high voltage greatly reduces current and therefore greatly reduces energy wasted as heat in the cables during transmission.

practice_questions.text: The UK government is considering whether to build more hydroelectric power stations in mountainous regions. Evaluate whether this is a good decision for energy supply and the environment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): explains that hydroelectric is reliable (not intermittent), renewable, produces no CO₂ during operation and can respond quickly to demand changes; identifies specific environmental costs (flooding of valleys, displacement of communities, disruption of river ecosystems, loss of habitat); acknowledges that the scale of impact depends on location and design; weighs the benefits (reliable, low-carbon electricity) against the costs (ecological and social harm); considers alternatives (offshore wind, nuclear) and whether there are better options; reaches a justified conclusion.
Secure (3–4): identifies advantages and disadvantages with some explanation; partial evaluation.
Developing (2): lists advantages and disadvantages without evaluation.
Emerging (1): one relevant point.

practice_questions.text: State what type of current the National Grid uses for long-distance transmission of electricity.
practice_questions.marks: Alternating current (AC). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the energy transfers that occur in a gas-fired power station, starting from the burning of fuel and ending with electricity entering the National Grid.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: One energy transfer correctly described (e.g. fuel burns releasing thermal energy).
Secure: Two transfers described correctly (e.g. fuel releases thermal energy; steam drives turbine converting to kinetic energy).
Mastering: Full sequence described: chemical energy in fuel → thermal energy (steam) → kinetic energy (turbine) → electrical energy (generator). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at very high voltage rather than at a lower voltage. Include the relevant equation in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: States that high voltage reduces energy loss.
Developing: Explains that high voltage means lower current (1 mark); states that lower current means less heat lost in cables (1 mark).
Secure: Uses P = I²R to explain that because current is squared, a small decrease in current gives a large decrease in power loss (1 mark).
Mastering: All three marks awarded with clear causal language and equation cited. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A step-up transformer at a power station has 500 turns on the primary coil and 50,000 turns on the secondary coil. The input voltage is 400 V. Calculate the output voltage. Suggest why this output voltage is suitable for transmission through the National Grid.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Identifies the turns ratio (1 mark: N_s/N_p = 100).
Secure: Calculates correct output voltage (1 mark: 400 × 100 = 40,000 V). Suggests that high voltage reduces current and therefore reduces energy losses in cables (1 mark).
Mastering: Full correct calculation shown and linked to P = I²R to justify the choice. Recognises that lower current means less heat dissipated in resistance of cables (4 marks). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: A wind farm produces 2 MW of electrical power. The cables connecting it to the National Grid have a total resistance of 5 Ω. Calculate the power lost as heat when the electricity is transmitted at a current of 40 A. Evaluate whether this is an acceptable level of loss.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: Uses correct equation P = I²R (1 mark).
Secure: Correct calculation: 40² × 5 = 8000 W = 8 kW (1 mark). Compares 8 kW to 2 MW = 2000 kW, concluding loss is small (0.4%) (1 mark).
Mastering: Evaluates acceptability using percentage loss and identifies that the National Grid achieves this by stepping up voltage before transmission (1 mark). [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the advantages and limitations of using the National Grid to distribute electricity across the country. In your answer, consider both the physics of transmission and wider practical factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: Identifies one advantage or limitation with minimal development.
Developing: Describes one advantage (e.g. efficient because high-voltage transmission reduces heat losses) and one limitation (e.g. infrastructure cost; dependence on grid during power cuts) with basic explanation.
Secure: Explains the physics of high-voltage transmission using I²R; discusses a second advantage (e.g. can redirect supply to areas of high demand); discusses a practical limitation (e.g. time and cost of installing underground cables; visual impact of pylons).
Mastering: Developed evaluation of at least two advantages and two limitations, with clear use of physics reasoning for the transmission argument, and a reasoned judgement about whether the advantages outweigh the limitations. [6 marks — levels marked]

practice_questions.text: Name one physical property that would be important when choosing a material for a frying pan handle.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any one of: low thermal conductivity (so it does not get hot); high melting point or does not soften at high temperature; hard/rigid/stiff (stays in shape under force). Developing: names a property without relevance to the context. Emerging: vague. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a life cycle assessment (LCA).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: an analysis that evaluates the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life, from raw material extraction to disposal. Secure: covers all stages of product life, assessing environmental impact. Developing: considers environmental impact of a product. Emerging: looking at how eco-friendly something is.

practice_questions.text: Explain why reusing a product has a lower environmental impact than recycling it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: reusing extends the life of the product without any reprocessing, so no energy is needed for collection, sorting, melting or reforming; recycling requires collection, transport, sorting and reprocessing, all of which use energy and may produce waste or emissions; therefore reuse avoids these energy costs entirely. Secure: reuse needs no energy for processing, recycling does — two clear points. Developing: reuse is better for the environment with one reason. Emerging: reusing saves materials.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is deciding whether to make a sports drinks bottle from glass or PET plastic. Compare the properties and LCA considerations of each material and suggest which would be more suitable. Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: glass is heavier, higher density (less suitable for sports use), does not leach chemicals, high melting point so can be sterilised, but is brittle and heavier; PET is lighter (important for portability), tough, transparent, can be recycled; LCA: glass can be reused many times and recycled; PET uses crude oil feedstock (finite) but is lightweight (less transport energy); justified conclusion relating to the sports context (likely PET for lightweight, shatterproof use). Secure: two relevant property comparisons, one LCA point, reasoned conclusion. Developing: compares one property. Emerging: names one material without comparison.

practice_questions.text: A recycling company claims that making a cotton tote bag has a lower environmental impact than making a plastic carrier bag. A journalist argues the opposite, citing a government LCA report. Evaluate which source is likely to be more reliable and explain what an LCA would need to include to settle the argument.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: recycling company has a financial interest in promoting the cotton bag so may cherry-pick data; government LCA report is more likely to be independent and peer reviewed but may still be limited by data availability; to settle the argument the LCA needs to include: all four stages (extraction, manufacture, use and disposal) for both products; energy use, water use, greenhouse gas emissions and biodegradability at each stage; typical number of uses per bag; disposal route (landfill, incineration, recycling, composting); the cotton bag uses more water in cotton farming and more energy in manufacture, but is biodegradable; the plastic bag uses less water and energy in manufacture but is non-biodegradable and is derived from a finite resource; conclusion must acknowledge subjectivity and note that the answer depends on usage pattern and disposal. Secure: identifies bias in company data; names three LCA components; one comparison between bag types. Developing: identifies one source as more reliable with one reason; names two LCA stages. Emerging: mentions LCA without critical evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Suggest why PET drinks bottles can be economically recycled, but some other plastic products cannot.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: PET bottles are produced in very large quantities so are abundant in the waste stream; they are easy to identify and sort; the market for recycled PET (fibres, new bottles) is well established; some other plastics are produced in smaller quantities, are harder to sort (mixed compositions), or have little market for recycled material — making collection and processing economically unviable. Secure: abundance in waste stream, ease of sorting, and/or established market. Developing: PET is common and has a use. Emerging: vague.

practice_questions.text: A block of material has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
Describe what happens to the temperature of a substance during a change of state, and explain why.
practice_questions.marks: The temperature does not change during a change of state [1 mark]. The energy supplied is used to break the forces between particles (changing their arrangement), not to increase their kinetic energy [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States temperature stays constant but gives no explanation in terms of particles.

practice_questions.text: A 3 kg copper block is cooled from 200 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of copper is 385 J/kg/°C. Calculate the energy released by the block.
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: Correctly identifies the temperature change and substitutes into the equation but makes an arithmetic error.

practice_questions.text: A kettle contains 1.5 kg of water at 20 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4,200 J/kg/°C. Calculate the energy needed to bring the water to 100 °C. Then calculate the additional energy needed to boil the water away completely. The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2,260,000 J/kg.
practice_questions.marks: Energy to heat: ΔE = 1.5 × 4200 × (100 − 20) = 1.5 × 4200 × 80 = 504,000 J [1 mark]. Energy to vaporise: E = m × L = 1.5 × 2,260,000 = 3,390,000 J [1 mark]. Total energy = 504,000 + 3,390,000 = 3,894,000 J [1 mark]. The vaporisation energy is much larger than the heating energy [1 mark — accept comparison that latent heat of vaporisation >> heat energy for same mass].
practice_questions.marks_rubric:
Secure: Both energies calculated correctly, comparison made.
Developing: Heating energy correct but error in latent heat calculation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why an object with an average density less than water will float, using the equation for density in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Density = mass ÷ volume [1 mark]. If an object's average density is less than 1,000 kg/m³ (the density of water), it displaces a weight of water equal to its own weight before it is fully submerged [1 mark], so the upward force of the water (upthrust) balances its weight and it floats [1 mark].
practice_questions.marks_rubric: Developing: States that lower density objects float but does not connect to density equation or displaced water.

practice_questions.text: A student heats equal masses of water and vegetable oil using identical heaters. The oil heats up faster. Evaluate what this tells us about the specific heat capacities of the two substances, and explain one practical application of this difference.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Uses ΔE = mcΔΘ — for the same ΔE (same heater, same time) and same m, a larger ΔΘ means smaller c. Therefore vegetable oil has a lower SHC than water. Quantifies the reasoning: if oil heats twice as fast, its SHC is half that of water. Explains a practical application: water's high SHC makes it ideal as a coolant in car engines (absorbs large amounts of thermal energy per kg without large temperature rise) or in central heating systems (transports large amounts of thermal energy). Alternatively: cooking in oil is faster because oil's lower SHC allows it to reach higher temperatures more quickly with less energy input.
Secure: Correctly deduces oil has lower SHC using the equation; gives one valid application.
Developing: Correctly deduces oil has lower SHC but without reference to the equation; application unclear.
Emerging: States oil heats faster without connecting to SHC.

practice_questions.text: State the relative charge of a neutron.
practice_questions.marks: Zero (accept 0 or neutral).

practice_questions.text: Describe what isotopes are and give one example.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons; gives a correct example (e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14, both with 6 protons but 6 and 8 neutrons respectively).
Secure: Correct definition and a valid example.
Developing: Correct definition but no example, or example given without clear explanation.
Emerging: Vague description without reference to proton/neutron numbers.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the results of Rutherford’s alpha particle scattering experiment led to the nuclear model of the atom.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Describes the observation (most particles passed through; some deflected at large angles; very few bounced back); links each observation to a conclusion (mostly empty space; concentrated positive charge; small, dense nucleus); explains why these results could not be explained by the plum pudding model.
Secure: Two observations linked correctly to conclusions.
Developing: One correct observation-conclusion link.
Emerging: General statement about Rutherford without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: An atom of element X has mass number 40 and atomic number 20. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom of X. Compare this with an isotope of X that has mass number 42.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly states 20 protons, 20 neutrons, 20 electrons for the first atom; correctly states that the isotope has 20 protons, 22 neutrons, 20 electrons; explicitly notes what is the same (proton number, electron number, chemical properties) and what is different (mass number, neutron number).
Secure: Correct numbers for both atoms with some comparison.
Developing: Correct numbers for one atom; comparison attempted but incomplete.
Emerging: One or two numbers correct; no meaningful comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Bohr model was an improvement on Rutherford’s nuclear model.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that Rutherford’s model could not explain why electrons did not spiral into the nucleus (classical physics predicts accelerating charges emit radiation and lose energy); Bohr proposed electrons occupy fixed energy levels at specific distances; electrons can only have certain energies, not arbitrary ones; this explained stability of atoms and atomic emission spectra.
Secure: Identifies that Bohr introduced fixed energy levels and explains what problem this solved.
Developing: States that Bohr added energy levels but does not explain what was improved.
Emerging: Names Bohr without explaining the improvement.

practice_questions.text: A student claims: ‘Rutherford’s nuclear model proved that all atoms have a small, dense, positive nucleus.’ Evaluate this claim, using your knowledge of how scientific models develop.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains what the gold-foil experiment showed (observations and conclusions); explains that the nuclear model provided a better explanation than the plum pudding model; but notes that ‘proved’ is too strong a word — the model was a better fit for the available evidence, not proof; discusses how Bohr later refined the model because the nuclear model alone could not explain electron stability; concludes that science produces models that best fit current evidence, not absolute proofs; models are revised when better evidence or explanations emerge.
Secure: Describes the experiment and its implications; notes that scientific models are provisional; some discussion of model revision.
Developing: Describes the experiment but does not engage with the philosophical point about proof vs best fit.
Emerging: Basic description of the experiment without evaluative reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Name the two types of particle found in the nucleus of an atom.
practice_questions.marks: Protons and neutrons. [1 mark — both required]

practice_questions.text: Describe the differences between alpha and gamma radiation in terms of their ionising power and penetrating power.
practice_questions.marks: Alpha is strongly ionising but weakly penetrating (stopped by paper/few cm of air) [1 mark]. Gamma is weakly ionising but strongly penetrating (requires thick lead or concrete to significantly reduce it) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A radioactive source has an initial activity of 1 600 Bq and a half-life of 5 hours. Calculate the activity after 20 hours, showing each step.
practice_questions.marks: 20 hours = 4 half-lives [1 mark]. 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq [1 mark for correct repeated halving]. Final activity = 100 Bq [1 mark].

practice_questions.text:
Complete and balance the following nuclear equation for the alpha decay of radium-226 (atomic number 88), and suggest what element is produced.
²²⁶₈₈Ra → _____ + ⁴₂He
practice_questions.marks: Mass number of product = 226 − 4 = 222 [1 mark]. Atomic number of product = 88 − 2 = 86 [1 mark]. Equation: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆X + ⁴₂He [1 mark for correct notation]. Element with atomic number 86 is radon (Rn) [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: A scientist measures the count rate of a radioactive sample over time and obtains the following readings (after subtracting background): 2 400, 1 200, 600, 300 counts/min at 0, 2, 4 and 6 minutes respectively. Determine the half-life of the source and evaluate whether you can be confident this is an accurate value, considering the nature of radioactive decay.
practice_questions.marks: Half-life = 2 minutes (activity halves every 2 minutes) [1 mark]. Mastering (5–6): Correct half-life with evidence from data (showing each halving step). Evaluation: radioactive decay is random, so individual readings vary. A single set of measurements may not give an accurate half-life due to random fluctuations in count rate. To improve confidence: repeat the experiment several times and calculate a mean; use longer measurement periods for each reading to smooth out random variations; ensure background radiation has been correctly subtracted each time. The calculated half-life is most reliable when activity is still relatively high (many decays per unit time), as random variation becomes proportionally larger at lower activities. Secure (3–4): Correct half-life + partial evaluation. Developing (1–2): Correct half-life only.

practice_questions.text: Explain why alpha radiation is considered most dangerous when a source is inside the body, even though it is the least penetrating type of radiation.
practice_questions.marks: Alpha particles are the most ionising — they transfer a large amount of energy to nearby cells over a very short distance [1 mark]. When inside the body, the source is in direct contact with living tissue, so the low penetrating power is no longer protective [1 mark]. The intense ionisation can cause significant DNA damage, increasing the risk of mutation or cancer [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by 'herd immunity'.
practice_questions.marks: A level of immunity in a population where enough individuals are immune that a pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting even those who are not immune. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how antibodies destroy pathogens in the body.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: Any two of — antibodies clump pathogens together (agglutination) making them easier to engulf; antibodies neutralise toxins produced by pathogens; antibodies mark pathogens for destruction by phagocytes. [1 mark per mechanism described, 2 marks maximum.]

practice_questions.text: Explain why antibiotics are effective against bacterial infections but not against viral infections.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Antibiotics work by targeting bacterial structures such as the cell wall that are not present in human cells; viruses do not have cell walls and do not have independent cellular machinery, because they replicate inside the host cell using the host's own ribosomes and enzymes; since there are no bacterial-specific structures for the antibiotic to target in a viral infection, it has no effect.
Secure: Antibiotics target bacterial structures (e.g. cell wall) absent in viruses; viruses use host cell machinery so antibiotics cannot reach them.
Developing: Antibiotics work on bacteria not viruses because viruses are different.
Emerging: Antibiotics only kill bacteria.

practice_questions.text: Explain how antibiotic resistance develops in a bacterial population, using the idea of natural selection.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Random mutations in bacteria occasionally produce variants with reduced sensitivity to an antibiotic. When antibiotics are used, susceptible bacteria are killed, but resistant mutants survive. The resistant bacteria reproduce and pass the resistance to offspring. Over time, resistant forms become dominant in the population. Incomplete courses or overuse accelerates this process by selecting for resistant strains without eliminating them.
Secure: Mutation → resistance; antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survive and reproduce; resistance becomes common.
Developing: Some bacteria are resistant; they survive when antibiotics are used and breed.
Emerging: Bacteria become resistant over time.

practice_questions.text: A new drug for treating a bacterial lung infection is being trialled. The trial uses a double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Suggest why this design is used and what it controls for.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Double-blind means neither patients nor researchers know who receives the drug or the placebo; this removes researcher bias in recording improvements and removes the placebo effect (patients feeling better simply because they believe they are being treated). The placebo ensures any improvement in the drug group can be attributed to the drug itself rather than the psychological effect of receiving treatment. The design produces objective, unbiased evidence.
Secure: Removes researcher bias; controls for placebo effect; explains why each is important.
Developing: Stops patients or researchers knowing who has which, so results are fair.
Emerging: It makes the trial more fair.

practice_questions.text: Vaccination programmes have greatly reduced the incidence of several diseases, including measles. Evaluate the importance of high vaccination uptake in a community for protecting individuals who cannot receive the vaccine, such as newborn babies.
practice_questions.marks:
