Mastering: Explains what a balanced symbol equation shows (which substances react and form, in what ratio, physical states via state symbols, conservation of mass); evaluates limitations (equations do not show rate of reaction, activation energy, conditions required, three-dimensional arrangement of atoms, or the mechanism of how bonds break and form); compares word equations (more accessible, less informative) with symbol equations (precise, quantitative, universal language of chemistry); discusses how half-equations extend symbol equations to show electron transfer explicitly; reaches a balanced conclusion about the value of equations as communication tools.
Secure: At least four valid points about what equations do and do not show, with some evaluative language.
Developing: Three points about what equations show; limited evaluation of what is missing.
Emerging: Describes equations briefly without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: State Newton’s first law of motion.
practice_questions.marks: Award: an object remains stationary or continues at constant speed in a straight line unless acted on by a resultant force. Accept equivalent correct wording.

practice_questions.text: A wave in a ripple tank has a frequency of 5 Hz and a wavelength of 0.04 m. Calculate its speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: correct equation stated and correct answer 0.2 m/s with unit.
Secure: correct method, minor arithmetic error.
Developing: equation recalled but substitution error.
Emerging: equation not recalled or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: A 1200 kg car accelerates at 3 m/s². Explain what is meant by resultant force and calculate the resultant force acting on the car.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: resultant force defined as the net or combined force taking direction into account (1), F = ma stated (1), correct answer 3600 N (1).
Secure: correct calculation but incomplete definition.
Developing: definition given but calculation error.
Emerging: definition only or equation only.

practice_questions.text: A crumple zone at the front of a car extends the time for a collision from 0.05 s to 0.25 s. Compare the forces the driver experiences in each case if their change in momentum is 900 kg m/s. Explain your answer using physics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: F = Δp ÷ Δt used (1), force without crumple zone = 900 ÷ 0.05 = 18,000 N (1), force with crumple zone = 900 ÷ 0.25 = 3,600 N (1), clear explanation linking longer time to smaller force for same change in momentum (1).
Secure: both forces correct, explanation incomplete.
Developing: one force correct, method shown.
Emerging: equation stated but not applied.

practice_questions.text: A radio station broadcasts electromagnetic waves at a speed of 3 × 10⁸ m/s with a wavelength of 1500 m. Calculate the frequency of the broadcast. Give your answer in standard form.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: f = v ÷ λ = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 1500 = 2 × 10⁵ Hz, with unit.
Secure: correct method, arithmetic error.
Developing: equation stated but rearrangement incorrect.
Emerging: no valid method.

practice_questions.text: Newton’s second law can be expressed as \(F = ma\) or as \(F = \Delta p \div \Delta t\). Discuss how both forms are useful and explain how the concept of momentum helps engineers design safer vehicles. Use specific calculations or examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: both equations stated and linked (2), specific example of safety feature using \(F = \Delta p \div \Delta t\) with correct reasoning (2), quantitative or qualitative comparison of forces showing safety benefit (2).
Secure: both equations, good safety feature explanation, limited quantitative support.
Developing: one equation applied, partial safety reasoning.
Emerging: identifies that time affects force without using equations.

practice_questions.text: Name the colour produced in a flame test for potassium ions.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: lilac (accept: purple).

practice_questions.text: Describe the test for carbon dioxide gas and the observation that confirms its presence.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: bubble the gas through limewater. 1 mark: limewater turns milky / cloudy (because calcium carbonate precipitates).

practice_questions.text: Explain how you would distinguish between a solution containing aluminium ions and one containing magnesium ions using sodium hydroxide solution.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: add sodium hydroxide solution to both — both produce a white precipitate. 1 mark: add excess sodium hydroxide. 1 mark: the aluminium precipitate dissolves (amphoteric) but the magnesium precipitate does not dissolve.

practice_questions.text: In a chromatography experiment, the solvent front travels 15.0 cm and a dye spot travels 9.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value for the dye and suggest what this tells a chemist about the dye.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Rf = 9.0 ÷ 15.0 = 0.60. 1 mark: Rf values are between 0 and 1 / this value can be compared with reference Rf values to identify the substance. 1 mark: a pure substance has a single spot with a characteristic Rf under the same conditions. 1 mark: if the Rf matches a known substance under the same conditions, the dye is likely to be that substance.

practice_questions.text: A forensic scientist needs to identify an unknown white powder. Describe how they would use chemical tests to identify both the cation and anion present, and explain why a systematic approach is important.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Describes dissolving the sample; flame test to suggest cation; NaOH precipitate to confirm cation (stating colour and any effect of excess NaOH); explains why both tests together are more reliable than one alone; describes appropriate anion test (silver nitrate for halide after acidifying with HNO₃, or barium chloride for sulfate after acidifying with HCl); explains that a systematic approach prevents missing evidence or drawing incorrect conclusions from one test alone.
Secure (3–4): Describes most steps correctly with some explanation of why the approach is reliable.
Developing (2): Identifies some tests but links are poorly explained or sequence is unclear.
Emerging (1): Recalls one test with no systematic structure.

practice_questions.text: Compare traditional chemical tests with instrumental methods such as gas chromatography–mass spectrometry for identifying substances.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: traditional tests are cheaper / use simple equipment. 1 mark: instrumental methods are more sensitive and can detect trace amounts. 1 mark: instrumental methods are faster and can be automated. 1 mark: instrumental methods give quantitative / more accurate results whereas traditional tests give qualitative observations only. [Any 4 valid comparative points, each clearly comparing the two approaches.]
